c0fa6f84e9ccebd1: WASHINGTON: The Unites States Transportation Department on Monday will finalise sharply lower vehicle fuel economy standards through 2031, reversing a push by the Biden administration ​to force automakers to build more electric vehicles, officials said on Saturday.

President Donald Trump said he had approved new fuel economy standards for cars and trucks, which he said will lower the price of new vehicles. "A major victory for America's auto workers is coming Monday," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.
The new standards would cut the cost of new vehicles but increase fuel consumption and carbon dioxide emissions for decades, according to the department's own estimates.
Trump's push comes as American drivers are grappling with sharply higher fuel prices since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran at the end of February.

Under Democratic President Joe Biden, the government sought to push automakers to build more electric vehicles to meet rising fuel-efficiency standards. Biden increased required fuel efficiency for cars ‌by ⁠8.0 per cent annually for model years 2024 and 2025, 10 per cent for 2026 and 2.0 per cent annually from 2027 to 2031.
The Trump administration in December proposed retroactively revising down the 2022 model year fuel economy standard ​and then raising it between 0.25 per cent and 0.5 per cent annually through 2031.

The Transportation Department proposed a fleetwide average of 34.5 miles per gallon (14.7 km per litre) by ​2031, down from 50.4 miles per gallon (21.4 km per litre) under Biden. It estimated its proposal would cut average new ​vehicle costs by US$930 each.
But it would increase fuel consumption by ​around 100 ⁠billion gallons through 2050, fuel spending by US$185 billion and carbon dioxide emissions by about 5.0 per cent, the department said.

Trump's move will make it easier for automakers to sell consumers less efficient vehicles. "Lowering standards will accelerate what (Trump) has already been doing: handing the clean tech future to China and forcing Americans to pay more at the pump," said Pete Buttigieg, who headed the Transportation Department under Biden.
Biden focused on reducing US greenhouse gas emissions and fossil fuel use, accelerating a transition to clean energy and making the US. a global leader ​in clean-energy technology and manufacturing.
643ab07ffe7683dd: ELINA Svitolina punctuated Ukraine's first trip to the Billie Jean King Cup final by triumphantly slamming her racket to the court Saturday in Shenzhen, China.
Svitolina sealed a 2-0 win against two-time defending champion Italy with a 6-2, 6-2 victory against Jasmine Paolini in the semifinals of the women's team tennis competition.
Anhelina Kalinina had given Ukraine the lead with a 6-3, 6-4 victory against Tyra Caterina Grant. Sunday's opponent in the final is the Czech Republic, which defeated Spain 2-0 on Friday.
No. 6 seed Leylah Fernandez of Canada rallied for a 1-6, 6-4, 6-2 victory against No. 5 Maja Chwalinska of Poland in a semifinal match that lasted two hours and eight minutes.

Fernandez trailed 4-3 in the second set before launching her comeback, including a crucial break in the ninth game of the second set. Both players converted five of eight break points in a tightly contested match, with Fernandez posting a 72-69 edge in total points won.

Fernandez will face unseeded Australian Talia Gibson in the final of the WTA 500 tournament on Sunday. Gibson advanced in a walkover when Russia's Tatiana Prozorova withdrew after sustaining a concussion during a doubles match.
No. 2 seed Kimberly Birrell and No. 5 Maya Joint will meet in a rare all- Australian final following a busy day in Seoul.
It is the first time two Aussies have clashed for a WTA Tour title since Strasbourg in 2017 (Samantha Stosur defeated Daria Gavrilova) and just the third such final in the 21st century.
After rain interrupted play on Friday, Birrell completed her 2-6, 6-2, 7-5 quarterfinal win against Katie Volynets before outlasting No. 6 Anna Bondar of Hungary 7-5, 2-6, 6-1 in the semifinals.
Joint knocked out No. 3 Lanlana Tararudee of Thailand 6-4, 6-3 in the quarterfinals and was leading 6-2, 1-0 when Russia's Alina Korneeva was forced to retire from their semifinal match. — REUTERS
7d80a91c579a27d7: MADRID, Sept 27 — Thousands of people marched through Madrid yesterday to protest the eviction earlier this week of an 87-year-old woman from her lifelong home, calling for greater protection for tenants.

Images of Maricarmen Abascal being carried from her Madrid flat on a stretcher on Wednesday after police broke down her door have thrust Spain’s housing crisis back into the spotlight ahead of a general election due in 2027.
Protesters rattled keys, blew whistles, chanted slogans and held banners calling for measures to curb rising housing costs and make evictions more difficult as they marched through central Madrid.
“You could be the next Maricarmen,” read one banner.
Enrique Ortega de Miguel, a 38-year-old graphic designer who lives with his mother, said the housing market in Spain was “impossible”.
“It is a struggle to find a place you can afford, then you live in fear of being forced out,” he told AFP at the protest.
Government authorities put the turnout at around 25,000, while organisers of the protest said 300,000 participated.
“Maricarmen’s eviction has caused outrage and marks a turning point,” Alicia del Rio, spokesman for the Madrid Tenants’ Union, told reporters at the start of the march which ended outside parliament.
Abascal, who has become a symbol of Spain’s housing crisis, urged Spaniards to join the protest in a video message posted online just hours before it got underway.
“I want what has happened to me to serve so that it does not happen to other people,” she said from hospital, where she has been treated for exhaustion since her eviction.
“I want it to encourage people to fight and to help change the laws that have allowed me to be evicted,” she added in the video, posted by the tenants’ union.
‘Fed up’

Abascal was forced to leave the apartment where she had lived for 70 years after a real estate firm acquired the property and raised the rent by 275 per cent to €2,650 (RM12,316), according to the union.
Irene Lopez, a 33-year-old engineer, said the situation “has become unsustainable”.
“There are people who can’t afford to live in cities, rents are out of step with salaries,” she told AFP, describing the eviction of Maricarmen as “the last straw”.
Another protester, Maricarmen Arnedo, a 76-year-old pensioner, said while older people were being forced out of their homes, “young people can’t move out of their parents’ homes”.
“We want house prices and rents to come down, because I’m fed up with washing the underpants of my 53-year-old son,” she added.
‘Social tragedy’

Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who last year pledged to make housing a government priority, is under growing pressure to act. There have been regular protests across Spain since Abascal’s eviction.
He has called Abascal’s eviction a “social tragedy that we cannot accept”.

The government is expected to approve a package of measures dubbed the “Maricarmen decree” at its next cabinet meeting, including the automatic renewal of rental contracts and further restrictions on evictions.
But it is unclear whether the package will be approved by parliament, where Sanchez’s government lacks a majority.
While a similar bill was defeated earlier this year, Abascal’s case has increased pressure on political parties to act.
The Bank of Spain estimates the country of around 50 million people is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.
Spain has little public housing, while rents have been driven up by increased demand, including from tourism and population growth linked to immigration, analysts say. — AFP
7638886d74cbe619: NEW YORK, Sept 27 — The United Nations (UN) must move from reacting to crises to preventing them, with the task particularly urgent in Gaza, Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan said.
He said the UN should not merely respond after disasters had occurred by counting the dead, delivering supplies and rebuilding what had been destroyed, only to wait for the next crisis.
“This cannot be the future of multilateralism. We must move from reaction to prevention,” he said in his national statement at the General Debate of the 81st UN General Assembly here on Saturday.
Mohamad said nowhere was that task more urgent than in Gaza.
He said Malaysia and many other member states had exhausted every effort in the pursuit of justice for Gaza, including consistently calling for an immediate ceasefire and unrestricted supply of aid.
“We have supported humanitarian work in Palestine. We have pushed for punitive action towards Israel. And we have advocated for full Palestinian membership in this Hall,” he said.
However, he said the collective will of the General Assembly had repeatedly encountered the silencing effect of the veto.
“Malaysia will speak plainly: We are sick of it,” he said.
Mohamad said Malaysia would continue to support efforts to strengthen the multilateral system and ensure that it could respond effectively to conflicts and humanitarian crises.
According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 174,000 injured in Gaza since October 2023.
The foreign minister is in New York from Sept 23 to 27 for Malaysia’s participation in the 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA). — Bernama

73122f1d91ce04ae: KUALA LUMPUR: The ringgit is expected to trade within a narrow range against the US dollar next week as investors await key United States economic data for further clues on the direction of interest rates.

Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said attention would be on the US labour market next week, particularly the nonfarm payrolls report which is due to be released on Oct 2.
"We expect the ringgit to trade within a range of around RM4.07 to RM4.10 against the US dollar next week," he told Bernama.

Mohd Afzanizam said attention would also be on the US Personal Consumption Expenditures inflation report due on Sept 30, with consensus estimates pointing to an inflation rate of 3.7 per cent in September, unchanged from August.
On the domestic front, he said focus would increasingly turn to Budget 2027, which is scheduled to be tabled on Oct 9.
"Domestic political developments could also influence how foreign investors assess the Malaysian market, with the Melaka state election among the developments being monitored," he said.
Meanwhile, on a Friday-to-Friday basis, the ringgit increased against the greenback to 4.0715/0765 from 4.0795/0840 a week earlier.
The local currency also traded higher against a basket of major currencies during the week.

The ringgit appreciated versus the British pound to 5.3907/3973 from 5.4543/4603 on the previous Friday, gained against the Japanese yen to 2.5764/5797 from 2.5829/5860, and rose vis-a-vis the euro to 4.6378/6435 from 4.6849/6901.
It also traded mostly higher against Asean currencies.

The local note edged up versus the Singapore dollar to 3.1858/1900 from 3.1933/1971 a week earlier, strengthened vis-a-vis the Thai baht to 12.2036/2234 from 12.2383/2562, and climbed against the Indonesian rupiah to 227.4/227.8 from 229.7/230.0
However, it slipped against the Philippine peso to 6.52/6.53 from 6.50/6.51 last Friday.
3c25fe234fb20d75: BAKU, Sept 27 — George Russell resisted a late charge from Max Verstappen to claim his first lights-to-flag victory with a composed drive for Mercedes in yesterday’s thrilling Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

The 28-year-old Briton came home just 0.196 seconds ahead of the four-time champion with his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar third on his return after a broken wrist in a race punctuated by two safety cars.

It was Russell’s first win on the fast, challenging streets of Baku, his first since the Austrian Grand Prix in June,and the eighth of his career. It trimmed team-mate Kimi Antonelli’s lead in the drivers’ championship to 66 points.
Antonelli finished fifth behind Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc after slicing through the field from 16th on the grid. Seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton was sixth in the second Ferrari.
“It’s amazing to be back on the top step so I want to say a big thank you to the team for helping me through a tough moment,” said Russell.
“The first half of the race felt pretty plain sailing, getting the gap, but after the safety car I saw Max behind me and I knew it wasn’t going to be easy.
“When the yellow flag came out, I lifted off the power and when I came back I had no turbo and Max nearly got me on the line.”
“We had a good race,” he said. “In the final lap, George lost a bit of boost so that’s why I caught up quite a bit. It got close, but it wasn’t enough.”
“It’s been a very long six weeks since I injured myself, but it felt like the right moment to come back. I felt strong and this is my first proper podium finish on pure pace so I am delighted.”
Racing Bulls’ rookie Arvid Lindblad was seventh, Esteban Ocon eighth ahead of his Haas team-mate Oliver Bearman and Williams’ Carlos Sainz.

Russell made a near-perfect start from his 12th pole position to draw clear while, behind him, Oscar Piastri took advantage of a slow-starting Leclerc to take second. Antonelli dropped from 16th to 17th.
Verstappen also enjoyed the opening lap and passed both Alpines before powering past Hamilton, Norris, Leclerc and finally team-mate Hadjar to rise to third.
The Dutchman was grumbling about his tyres, but Russell on the same medium compound
4446d2b3384dc238: KUALA LUMPUR: Bursa Malaysia is expected to see bargain hunting next week, with the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) likely to trade within the 1,660-1,690 range, said an analyst.

Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd vice-president of equity research Thong Pak Leng said investors are expected to remain wary of the Malaysian market as elevated United States Treasury yields could continue to pressure regional fund flows, although the recent correction has brought selected blue-chip valuations to more attractive levels.
He said the market's direction would also depend on developments in global bond yields and investor risk appetite.

"With the FBM KLCI's relative strength index at around 35, near oversold territory, we expect bargain hunting to emerge in fundamentally strong heavyweights, particularly banks and defensive names, should external conditions stabilise.
"Nevertheless, 1,670 remains a key resistance level, which could cap the near-term recovery," he told Bernama.
Thong said attention would also turn to China's Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) and the US employment report, which could influence regional risk appetite and the direction of bond yields.

For the week ended yesterday, bargain hunting lifted the index early in the week, but gains were capped by elevated US Treasury yields, higher oil prices, geopolitical uncertainties and foreign selling.
The benchmark index ended marginally lower on Friday amid concerns over rising yields and escalating tensions in West Asia.
On a Friday-to-Friday basis, the FBM KLCI increased 6.06 points to 1,671.62 at yesterday's close, from 1,665.56 a week earlier.

On the index board, the FBM Emas Index rose 44.92 points to 12,456.64, the FBM Top 100 Index gained 33.09 points to 12,243.46, the FBM Emas Shariah Index shed 5.76 points to 12,306.23 and the FBM ACE Index expanded 288.26 points to 5,532.86, while the FBM Mid 70 Index gained 0.89 of a point to 17,844.91.

By sector, the Energy Index advanced 41.21 points to 861.83 and the Plantation Index erased 161.57 points to 9,334.87. The Industrial Products and Services Index slid 1.14 points to 184.1, while the Financial Services Index accumulated 137.86 points to 19,550.49.
Weekly turnover firmed to 17.11 billion units worth RM14.07 billion from 15.02 billion units worth RM14.18 billion in the previous week.
Main Market volume improved to 10.41 billion units valued at RM12.31 billion, from 9.38 billion units valued at RM12.93 billion previously.
Warrants turnover widened to 4.21 billion units worth RM661.61 million, from 3.61 billion units worth RM498.33 million in the previous week.
ACE Market volume garnered to 2.48 billion units valued at RM1.09 billion, compared with 2.02 billion units valued at RM748.59 million in the previous week.
b856f5050d2c3e4a: NEW YORK, Sept 27 — The veto power of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) must be challenged and ultimately abolished to address the Council’s failures, Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan said.

He said expanding the Council’s membership alone would not be enough to resolve its shortcomings, stressing that the use of the veto must be questioned and strongly challenged by every member of the UN General Assembly, particularly in cases involving crimes against humanity.

“The exercise of the veto must be questioned and strongly challenged by every single member of this General Assembly. Particularly in cases of crimes against humanity,” he said in his national statement at the General Debate of the 81st UN General Assembly here on Saturday.
Mohamad said Resolution 76/262 had already created an accountability channel between the Security Council and the General Assembly.
“We must make full use of this Resolution as a launchpad for greater accountability regarding the use of the veto,” he said.
He said the international community must begin work now to reform the Security Council.

“Expanding the Council’s membership alone will not be enough to resolve its failures. It is the veto that must be challenged, and it is the veto that must be abolished. We must begin the work now,” he said.
Mohamad said there was still time to save the global order, stressing that paralysis in the Security Council should not translate into paralysis of the United Nations.

He also highlighted the growing trust deficit confronting the UN, saying trust could only be restored through concrete action, including ensuring that international law was upheld and that people around the world continued to believe their voices mattered.
The UNSC is the United Nations’ principal body for addressing international peace and security, comprising 15 members, including five permanent members with veto power.
Mohamad is in New York from Sept 23 to 27 for Malaysia’s participation in the 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA). — Bernama
b8c0a458ea033a5a: THE International team finished strong Saturday to remain in front of the United States through three days of the Presidents Cup outside Chicago, holding a 10 1/2-7 1/2 lead.
Chris Gotterup and Cameron Young combined to win two matches for the US at Medinah Country Club's No. 3 course, creating at least some suspense for Sunday's final day.

In the last two matches to go complete in afternoon foursomes, New Zealand's Ryan Fox and Australia's Min Woo Lee upended Sam Burns and Wyndham Clark by 3 and 2 and then Canadians Corey Conners and Nick Taylor needed all 18 holes for a 1 up triumph against Russell Henley and Jacob Bridgeman.
The International tandem recovered from Taylor's tee shot into the rough on the last hole to post par and avoid halving the match.
Gotterup/Young rolled to a 6 and 4 victory against Australia's Adam Scott and South Korea's Sungjae.
Patrick Cantlay and Xander Schauffele edged South Korea teammates Tom Kim and Si Woo Kim by 2 and 1.
In morning four-ball, the US claimed a 2 1/2-1 1/2 edge to narrow its gap after the International team swept five foursomes matches Friday.
Gotterup/Young defeated Conners/Taylor by 2 and 1, while Scottie Scheffler and Burns had the same margin against Japan's Hideki Matsuyama and Ryo Hisatsune.
The International team prevailed 2 and 1 with Kim/Kim topping Collin Morikawa and Clark by 2 and 1.

Each team earned a half-point on a draw with Lee and Im vs. Justin Thomas and Jackson Koivun, but the US side failed to protect a 2 up lead. On No. 16, Lee/Im drew even despite a bogey because Thomas and Koivun each hit shots into the rough and couldn't recover. — REUTERS

5950197820f5920d: KOTA BHARU, Sept 27 — Children under 14 accounted for about 36 per cent of the 96 drowning deaths recorded in Kelantan since 2023, highlighting the urgent need to strengthen preventive measures and water safety awareness for this group.
Kelantan Fire and Rescue Department (JBPM) director Farhan Sufyan Borhan said out of the total fatalities, 35 victims were children, with the highest figure of 14 deaths recorded in 2024.
He said department statistics showed 28 drowning fatalities in 2023, rising to 31 in 2024, then declining to 27 in 2025, with 10 so far this year.
For victims under 14, seven deaths were recorded in 2023, followed by 14 cases in 2024, 11 cases in 2025, and three cases so far this year.

Consequently, Farhan Sufyan said Kelantan JBPM is increasing preventive efforts through water safety education and awareness, including the free Program Jom Renang (Let’s Swim Programme) conducted in five series involving 300 children under 12 at various locations statewide.
“This programme aims to equip children with basic swimming skills, water safety knowledge, and self-rescue techniques as proactive steps to reduce the risk of drowning incidents,” he said.

He also reminded parents to constantly monitor their children near rivers, ponds, lakes, and open bodies of water, stressing that cooperation from schools, communities, and the public is vital to embedding water safety practices to avert drowning tragedies. — Bernama
1d0c6260175fc343: JOHANNESBURG: Defenders Ime Okon and Samukele Kabini scored their first goals for South Africa in a tense 2-1 win over Guinea on Saturday in 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying.
Centre-back Okon, who plays for German second-tier club Hannover, hammered a loose ball into the net from close range to give the hosts a 30th-minute lead in Soweto.
Norway-based full-back Kabini, a second-half substitute for Aubrey Modiba, claimed the 77th-minute match-winner, racing through to beat goalkeeper Soumaila Sylla at his near post.
Guinea had equalised after 69 minutes when a free kick was not cleared and Seydouba Cisse reacted quickest to fire past captain Ronwen Williams.
The match marked the start of a second permanent spell in charge of South Africa for Pitso Mosimane, a three-time CAF Champions League-winning coach with Mamelodi Sundowns and Al Ahly.
He has inherited from retired Belgian tactician Hugo Broos a team good at retaining possession, but lacking clinical finishing.
Much of the pre-match focus was on Guinea striker Serhou Guirassy, a prolific scorer for Borussia Dortmund, but winger Aliou Balde posed a greater threat with his pace and footwork.
South Africa were the fifth of 10 African participants at the 2026 World Cup after Algeria, Democratic Republic of Congo, Ivory Coast and Morocco to begin AFCON qualifying with a win.
Egypt, Senegal and Tunisia drew and Cape Verde and Ghana lost.
Victory lifted South Africa to the top of Group D, ahead of Eritrea and Kenya, who drew 1-1 in Nairobi.
Nahom Girmai scored for the visitors in the first half and Ryan Ogam levelled on 87 minutes for Kenya, who will co-host the 2027 AFCON with Tanzania and Uganda.
Automatic qualifiers Kenya are in Group D to gain competitive match practice. Their presence leaves the other three teams competing for one place at the finals. — AFP

4768f57c443d9fa3: LONDON, Sept 27 — World champions Spain came from behind to beat England 3-2 in an entertaining Nations League encounter at Wembley yesterday, denying the hosts a cathartic win after their painful World Cup exit.
Victory for Luis de la Fuente’s men extends Spain’s astonishing unbeaten run to 39 matches — a record for a European team.
England got off to a nightmare start when Lamine Yamal pounced on a gaffe by defender Marc Guehi, and they could easily have been three goals down as silky Spain created multiple chances.

But England, criticised for their ultra-defensive tactics in their World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina, showed adventure of their own and got their reward in the 36th minute when Barcelona winger Anthony Gordon finished a fine team move.
Four minutes later Thomas Tuchel’s men were ahead after captain Harry Kane headed home Nico O’Reilly’s cross via a Marc Cucurella deflection.
Kane had a golden chance to give England a two-goal cushion from the penalty spot 10 minutes into the second half but slipped slightly, crashing his shot against the bar.
Spain, who beat England in the Euro 2024 final, took full advantage, with substitutes Alex Baena and Mikel Oyarzabal both scoring to turn the match around.
De la Fuente said he felt his team had largely been in control against “superpower” England and he was confident they would have come back even from 3-1 down.

Asked about his side’s long unbeaten run, he said: “These are sensational moments.... Numbers are one thing, objective indicators are what we see. But what is important is that we still want to grow, we still want to improve.”
Kane bemoaned England’s inability to sustain their best level for the whole game.
“I spoke before that we reached good levels at the World Cup but didn’t quite put a full 90 minutes together,” he told ITV. “Probably similar again today.”
Shaky start
England boss Thomas Tuchel was adamant ahead of the match that it did not signal a new start but will have been dismayed at his team’s nervy start.
Manchester City’s Guehi, with a chance to clear in the second minute, inexplicably turned back towards goalkeeper James Trafford, apparently unaware that Yamal was just behind him.
The teenager pinched the ball and curled a left-footed effort off the inside of the post.
Ferran Torres was in the thick of the action, with an effort ruled out for offside and another shot saved by Trafford, in for long-time number one Jordan Pickford.
He also squandered a golden opportunity with just the goalkeeper to beat.
Yamal then set up Dani Olmo, who flashed wide as Spain rued yet another miss.
England, who had showed plenty of promise down the wings, made the visitors pay with an incisive counter-attacking goal after winning the ball back deep in their own half.
Gordon was involved early in the move and surged forward, collecting Jude Bellingham’s pass to steer the ball decisively past goalkeeper Unai Simon.
And, with the atmosphere now totally changed, England were in front when Kane rose to head home.
Tuchel’s men started the second half brightly and had a chance to extend their lead from the spot when they were awarded a penalty for a Rodri foul on Bellingham following a VAR check.
But Kane hit the bar and England paid the price when Baena steered home on the hour mark after O’Reilly had given the ball away to Olmo.
Worse was to come for the home side when Baena turned provider for Oyarzabal, who dinked the ball over Trafford.
Spain host Croatia in their next Nations League Group A3 match on Tuesday while England travel to the Czech Republic. — AFP
18b56997a24ebdf9: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 27 — The Malaysia My Second Home (MM2H) programme generated RM8.85 billion in economic value between Oct 1, 2024 and Aug 31, 2026, including more than RM5 billion in property purchases and RM3.82 billion in fixed deposits.

Deputy Tourism, Arts and Culture Minister Chiew Choon Man said the programme received 7,650 new applications during the same period across the Platinum, Gold, Silver and Special Economic Zone categories.

“MM2H has shown immense potential in expanding Malaysia’s foreign direct investment. The programme has successfully brought in billions of ringgit into the country in a short period of time and has benefitted many sectors of our economy,” he said in a statement yesterday.
Chiew said China led the applications with 3,847, followed by Taiwan (1,054), Hong Kong (324), Singapore (287) and the United States (284).
To further expand the programme’s reach to key target markets such as Hong Kong, Japan and South Korea, the MM2H One Stop Centre will organise overseas sales missions to these regions.

Chiew also said he had met key MM2H industry players and stakeholders, including consultants, real estate, education, healthcare and banking specialists, at the 14th MM2H National Workshop 2026 organised by the Malaysia My Second Home Consultants Association yesterday to gather feedback.

“Every concern is taken note of, and the ministry works closely together with other ministries and agencies for practical solutions,” he said, reiterating the ministry’s commitment to regulatory compliance, transparency and integrity to maintain the programme’s global reputation. — Bernama

dc5ba3b1fae8eab0: KUALA LUMPUR, Sep 27 — In the never-ending, self-destructive pursuit of the newest, hottest, most viral food, we’ve forgotten the capacity of a run-of-the-mill, everyday meal to excite and satisfy — and, more than that, to jolt us awake from the AI-generated negative feedback loop we call our daily routine.
Or maybe that’s just me.
Every neighbourhood should have a place like that: a restaurant or a stall that keeps you well fed, even tantalises the senses, without drawing too much attention to itself.
Everyone should be able to grab breakfast there before heading out to face the horrors of the day, or come for a restorative lunch and leave refreshed and revitalised.
Bangsar’s Lucky Garden has had its share of places like these, especially in the Pusat Penjaja that the time-honoured Anuar Fish Head Curry calls home.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Madam Tim’s stall is located at Gerai 2, with a pretty hard-to-miss neon sign. — Picture by Ethan Lau
Madam Tim Chicken Rice is one of the centre’s newer vendors, only a few months in, serving the tried and tested classic working man’s food: chicken rice.
Madam Tim’s stall is on the other end of the hawker centre, nondescript and flanked by two drink stalls.
All three sport signs and posters indistinguishable from one another: the same unnatural, uncanny AI-generated food and drink imagery, smooth and devoid of anything remotely resembling life.
It’s become especially prevalent among food businesses recently, but there’s no value in moralising at independent operators for using it.
As long as the cost of human-generated visuals remains rightfully higher than slop, the catch-22 will persist.
Nobody wins — not the businesses, not us diners. Only a few ghoulish billionaires. Big chains using AI, though, can go do one.
The “madam” herself is the sole operator of the stall, which offers a choice of “normal” or “free-range” chicken, but only poached, with either rice or hor fun.
You could opt for the chicken thigh rice set and leave only RM9 poorer, or you could be like me and get the entire lower quarter for RM18.
The poached chicken has reasonably smooth skin, the flesh is succulent enough, and the bean sprouts below it are decently crunchy.
Nothing groundbreaking, but all still very satisfying.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A little of this stuff goes a long way, but just try stopping at only having a little. — Picture by Ethan Lau
Then she brings a jar each of chilli sauce and ginger paste; the former is similarly unremarkable, but the latter is pure, unadulterated dynamite.
Not because it is fiery and explosive, but because it is dynamite in the thrilling, electrifying sense.

Common enough to be relegated to an afterthought, the condiment can vary from a simple mixture of blended ginger and hot oil to the deep, dark reduction of ginger, garlic and scallions you can find at Kong Sai in Taman Paramount.
This belongs to neither camp; the chunks of ginger are rough and uneven, the colour sitting somewhere between brown and a strange grey.
Each bite is a hefty dose of sweet and savoury notes; the warm punch of ginger remains, but mellowed.
It’s hit after hit of balanced intensity.
She tells me she uses whole pieces of ginger, cooked down for hours with a mixture of soy sauce and oyster sauce, before pounding it by hand.
I spied a shallot or two, but I won’t tell.
I finished the whole jar. She noticed and offered to bring more.
I thanked her, sheepishly, and decided against indulging my greed any further.
Really, every neighbourhood should have its own Madam Tim. If you do, count yourself lucky. If you don’t, go looking. Because they’re still out there, in every neighbourhood — at least for now.

d40b8efc7246c2b1: SEPTEMBER 27 — According to the Department of Statistics Malaysia, Malaysia’s economy grew six per cent in the second quarter of 2026, the country’s strongest Q2 growth outside the pandemic period since 2014.
Unemployment stood at 3.0 per cent for the quarter, edging up only slightly from 2.9 per cent in Q1. Headline inflation rose to a modest 1.9 per cent.
By almost every conventional measure, the Malaysian economy is performing well.

Yet ask the rakyat, and the picture looks very different. There is a persistent sense that wages are not stretching as far as they used to, that costs keep climbing even as official inflation stays low, and that the prosperity in the national accounts simply is not showing up in household budgets.

A regional survey released this month found cost of living to be South-east Asia’s single biggest social concern, cited by 42 per cent of respondents, with Malaysia’s own optimism levels notably tempered by it.

Even the prime minister has acknowledged the mismatch. Announcing that same quarter of growth, Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim felt the need to add a caveat of his own: “While the headline economic indicators remain encouraging, we recognise that many Malaysians continue to face pressures from the cost of living.”
The economy is growing but the people are not feeling it. So, the million-dollar question is, why?
What follows is one attempt at an answer, not the final word on it. It starts with a simple observation: everyone is technically competing in the same race, but nobody is driving the same car.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The economy is growing but the people are not feeling it. So, the million-dollar question is, why? — Picture by Raymond Manuel
The F1 car

Bank Negara governor Datuk Seri Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour has been explicit about what is driving the headline figure: manufacturing strength on continued global demand for electrical and electronic components tied to artificial intelligence and data centre construction.
This is real, but narrow, dependent on capital-intensive investment, global supply chains, and a relatively small number of large export-oriented firms.
These are the F1 cars in Malaysia’s economic race, purpose-built for this exact moment in the global economy.
They cross the line first, and that part is real. But they also only ever had room for one driver.

A new data centre or expanded chip fabrication line creates high-value jobs for engineers and technicians, but it does not, in the short run, raise the income of a retail assistant in Kuching, a hawker stall operator in Chemor, or an administrative clerk in Johor Bahru.
The sedan
The same Q2 data also shows what the rest of the field is driving. Agriculture contracted 3.7 per cent, reversing from 2.6 per cent growth in Q1, on weak oil palm and fishing output.
Services eased slightly too, to 5.4 per cent, though it remains the largest single contributor to overall growth.

Mining is the exception worth an explanation. It rebounded to 10.2 per cent growth after contracting in Q1, but this tracks global energy prices amid the Middle East conflict, not any shift in the sector’s role for ordinary workers, as mining employs a small fraction of the workforce compared with agriculture, retail, or services.
None of these domestic-facing sectors are accelerating the way the AI-linked engine is, nor should they be expected to.

They are also where most of the workforce is employed. DOSM figures show MSMEs accounted for almost half of total employment in 2025, 48.7 per cent, or 8.09 million people, spread across retail, hospitality, agriculture, and small-scale manufacturing.
This is the sedan most working Malaysians are actually driving: reliable enough for daily use but never built to keep pace with an F1 car. Above all, the gap is not a matter of effort.
Same fuel, different costs
Roughly a year into BUDI95, Malaysia’s flagship fuel subsidy rationalisation, its lagging effects are starting to show.
Full rollout came in September 2025, followed by a further quota cut this past April, and it’s this ongoing tightening that distinguishes this lap of the race from Malaysia’s past two-speed moments.
The issue is not whether the policy makes sense, but how unevenly its impact lands. Every car runs on fuel, but a rise in fuel cost does not register the same way for every car.

Transport and logistics costs seep into nearly every other price, and when they rise for households no longer covered by blanket subsidies, the effect does not show up cleanly in the 1.9 per cent headline inflation figure.
It shows up instead in what many Malaysians experience as everyday inflation, food away from home, transport-dependent services, the small recurring costs of running a household or small business.

A household on the domestic-facing track, where income growth has been modest, experiences the same subsidy adjustment as a proportionally larger bite out of a budget that was not expanding to begin with.

The policy may be sound and necessary. Its distributional timing, arriving while one part of the economy surges and the other merely holds steady, is what turns a fiscally responsible reform into felt financial strain for a large share of the population.
To return to the analogy: the sedan feels this pinch immediately as its budget was never built with much margin.
The F1 car, by contrast, barely notices the same rise in fuel cost against a team budget running into the hundreds of millions a year.
Different cars need different pit strategies

To be clear, I am not arguing against subsidy rationalisation. Fiscal discipline, targeted subsidy reform, and Malaysia’s push to attract high-value AI and data centre investment are each sound policy directions on their own merits, and the second quarter’s figures reflect real, creditable achievement. This is not a case of Malaysia’s economic management having failed.

The issue is sequencing and absorption, not direction, and no amount of steady driving closes a gap between two fundamentally different machines. Something else may need to change the terms of the race.
Malaysia is not the first country to face this problem, a narrow, foreign-investment-driven engine generating headline growth the rest of the economy does not proportionately feel.

Ireland offers one parallel worth considering: a small number of multinational tech and pharmaceutical firms account for a strikingly large share of its corporate tax revenue, disconnected from activity in the rest of the Irish economy.

Dublin’s response, modelled explicitly on Norway’s sovereign wealth fund, has been to divert a portion of that windfall into long-term investment vehicles rather than spend it through the ordinary budget.

Notwithstanding, Ireland’s own fiscal watchdog has warned the government is saving too little of it and spending too much now, a reminder that the temptation to let the fast car keep everything it earns is not unique to any one country.

Malaysia’s version of this question, whether AI-linked investment and export revenue should be treated, in part, as a windfall to be channelled deliberately toward the rest of the field, deserves its own careful examination, one this piece does not attempt to settle.

A sedan does not become an F1 car by driving more carefully. Understanding where the growth is actually coming from, and where it has not yet reached, seems a reasonable place to start before anyone proposes how to bring the rest of the field closer to the front.
* Dr Mohd Zaidi Md Zabri is an Assistant Professor at the IIUM Institute of Islamic Banking and Finance (IIiBF), International Islamic University Malaysia.

9f0dba59080bc5af: NEW YORK: The United Nations (UN) must move from reacting to crises to preventing them, with the task particularly urgent in Gaza, Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan said.

d1311c0dbc2c4d28: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 27 — Hari Cuci Malaysia (HCM) 2026 set two new records in the Malaysia Book of Records (MBOR) yesterday through large-scale public mobilisation and recyclable material collection in a single day.

071004baf0cf3f89: WASHINGTON, Sept 27 — AFP teams in Washington, Tehran and New York US President Donald Trump yesterday rejected a truce deal proposed by Iran that Tehran said could have reopened the Strait of Hormuz to shipping within a week.
The waterway is key to the world’s energy supply and is now central to the conflict between the US and Iran, which is at a stalemate after nearly seven months.
“I reject their proposal,” Trump told reporters outside the White House. “They made a proposal but I’ve rejected it.”
“They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they’re losing so badly. They want to make a deal and I think that’s fine. I like making a deal too.”

Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian, who was on his way back to Tehran after attending the UN General Assembly in New York, told CBS News the proposal had been developed “in coordination” with supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, according to an excerpt from the video interview shared by Iranian media.

Iran’s plan calls for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon, according to Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who met earlier in the week with Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff.

He said the conditions were the same as those laid out in a memorandum of understanding signed with the US earlier this year, which called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.
On the seventh day of the truce, Iran would reopen Hormuz. Pezeshkian told CBS that the “process will begin from the very day they accept it”.

At the UN, Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan complained that the “international community has been absent” and failing to live up to the responsibility to keep the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab open.

“The kingdom rejects any party’s use of these vital passages as a tool for pressure, threat, or harm to the interests of states,” he said, stressing the waterways’ importance to global energy security.

His Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov, told member states that “Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilising this strategically important region.”

In New York, Pezeshkian met with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, according to his office, and said: “Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table but, given past experiences, it no longer trusts the US.”

Araghchi said at the UN: “Iran has conveyed to the US, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days.”
“The choice now rests with the US. Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure,” he added.
However, within hours of his comments The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump was sceptical that Tehran would meet his demands and expects to renew the US bombing campaign.
Trump also posted an image to his Truth Social platform of a map showing the Strait of Hormuz circled and labelled “Trump Strait”.
Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, was quoted by Tasnim news agency as saying: “We will not cease punishing the US until Iran’s seven conditions are met.”
Hostilities in Yemen
Mohebi had told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran’s demands.
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war, to reopen the strait and to launch talks on Iran’s nuclear programme.
But the deal broke down shortly afterwards when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.
Iran requires ships to obtain authorisation before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.
Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the US sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation. — AFP

187295bf05bcbc33: PETALING JAYA: Umno’s willingness to work with different political camps risks eroding its partners’ trust and undermining the durability of future alliances, analysts say.
Mazlan Ali of Universiti Teknologi Malaysia said the approach could offer electoral advantages, but warned that repeatedly changing direction could strain its relations with partners.
He said Umno risks being perceived by its potential allies as an unreliable partner and by the electorate as an untrustworthy party.
“Frequently changing course could lead to a breakdown in cooperation and political instability,” he told FMT.

Mazlan’s remarks came in response to Melaka Barisan Nasional chairman Ab Rauf Yusoh’s statement that the coalition remains open to discussions with all parties ahead of the state polls, with no electoral pact finalised so far.

At the federal level, BN remains part of the unity government alongside Pakatan Harapan, with BN chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi insisting in July that the coalition intends to retain its place in Putrajaya until the end of the parliamentary term.

However, BN partnered with Perikatan Nasional in the Aug 1 Negeri Sembilan election, with the two coalitions winning 25 of the 36 seats. BN secured 18 seats while PN won seven, including three captured by Hamzah Zainudin’s Wawasan.

Despite this, Hamzah was not invited to the recent Umno general assembly, although several senior PAS leaders attended as guests, prompting analysts to predict that Umno was exploring direct cooperation with PAS that could leave Wawasan on the sidelines.
Mazlan said these arrangements had generated resentment within PH and among its grassroots, resulting in calls for BN to leave the administration.
He expects Umno and BN to continue pursuing partnerships with different parties as they seek to rebuild their strength and regain political power.
Meanwhile, Syaza Shukri of International Islamic University Malaysia said uncertainty over future partnerships should not be attributed solely to Umno, as PAS was also keeping its options open.
She said both parties’ reluctance to make firm commitments suggested limited trust between the two.
Syaza said Umno would prefer to operate without partners, viewing electoral alliances primarily as a means of securing enough support to form a government.
She warned that joining a coalition would not guarantee Umno’s continued commitment if the party later felt threatened or saw a more favourable opportunity elsewhere.
“So I don’t see any of these ‘pacts’ as anything more than an electoral strategy in order to form a government, but things can definitely change, as they have happened many times before,” she said.

ebc4a0c6cf9d2f37: PETALING JAYA: Grey hair, fading memory and a little more creaking around the edges are familiar signs of getting older. But could a rather strange-looking marine animal offer scientists clues about whether some aspects of ageing might one day be slowed - or even reversed?
Researchers have been studying compounds called plasmalogens, which are found naturally in the human body as well as in high concentrations in "sea squirts".
Not familiar with them? These unusual marine animals belonging to the class "Ascidiacea" aren't commonly found on Malaysian menus. They are more frequently eaten in parts of Japan and South Korea.
According to a recent report on the study, plasmalogen supplements were linked with better memory, healthier connections between brain cells and less inflammation in the brain.
And in one of the study’s more eye-catching findings, older recipients of the supplements also grew thicker, glossier and darker hair.
Before anyone starts searching seafood markets for an anti-ageing dinner, there is a major catch: the research was conducted in mice, not people.
The potential in plasmalogens
Plasmalogens are a type of fat molecule that forms part of cell membranes. They are particularly abundant in the brain, heart and immune cells, but their levels tend to decline with age.
Lower levels have also been observed in neurodegenerative conditions including Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease, although that does not necessarily mean the decline causes those diseases.

For the study, the researchers gave aged female mice plasmalogens derived from sea squirts over a two-month period. To test memory and learning, the mice were then put through a water maze in which they had to remember the location of a hidden platform.

Older mice receiving the supplements performed better than untreated ageing mice and, in some measures, behaved more like younger animals. Their brains were found to have more and healthier-looking synapses, which allow nerve cells to communicate with one another.

The supplemented mice also showed less activation of microglia, immune cells in the brain that can contribute to inflammation. The researchers believe reducing this inflammation may have helped preserve the brain’s ability to communicate and form new connections.
The study further found signs of increased synaptic plasticity and neurogenesis - essentially, processes involved in maintaining, adapting and forming nerve cells and their connections.
Exactly how plasmalogens produced these effects remains unclear. One possibility is that they help maintain the flexibility of cell membranes, making communication between nerve cells more efficient.
The researchers have also suggested that plasmalogens might influence the gut microbiome, which in turn communicates with the brain through the so-called gut-brain axis.
Perhaps the most visually striking result was not in the brain at all: older mice receiving plasmalogens grew thicker and glossier coats, with new dark hair appearing compared with untreated animals.
While intriguing, it does not mean sea squirts are a cure for ageing or even grey hair.
Indeed, animal studies are useful for uncovering biological mechanisms, but many treatments that work impressively in mice fail to produce the same results in humans.

The experts would still need clinical trials to establish whether plasmalogen supplements improve cognition in people, what doses might be safe and effective, and whether long-term use carries any risks.
So, for now, sea squirts are less a fountain of youth than an unusual clue in the continuing scientific puzzle of how our brains age.
9b1f2f98b78dbd68: PETALING JAYA: Malaysia will ensure the Formula 1 Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix at Sepang race circuit takes place in a safe, smooth and welcoming environment for participants, officials and visitors, says home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail.
He said about 700 security and traffic management personnel will be deployed throughout the event.
This matter was among the key issues discussed during Saifuddin’s bilateral meeting with Bahrain’s interior minister General Shaikh Rashid Abdulla Al Khalifa in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.
The meeting was held on the sidelines of the 15th UN Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice, Bernama reported.
The Formula 1 Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix will take place at the Sepang International Circuit (SIC) from Oct 2 to 4, 2026.
Saifuddin, in a Facebook post, said Malaysia was honoured to welcome Bahrain and the international motorsports community to Sepang.
“The staging of this prestigious event is not merely about motorsports but also serves as a bridge to strengthen the cordial relations and ties between the people of Malaysia and Bahrain.”

Saifuddin said a dedicated immigration lane at the airport would also be provided for team crews and accredited personnel, while visa arrangements would be facilitated for foreign nationals wishing to attend the event.

Saifuddin said Malaysia and Bahrain also discussed ways to enhance cooperation in tackling terrorism and extremism, intelligence sharing, drug enforcement and detection, as well as border management and security to combat transnational threats.
81ae1b7baec181dd: NEW YORK: Boeing said it identified an issue with the 737 MAX jet’s navigation system that could increase pilot workload during landing and may delay the arrival of its latest narrowbody models.

“Last month, we informed all 737 operators about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario,” Boeing said in a statement. “We shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases.”

The US Federal Aviation Administration separately said it was convening a review board to determine whether the glitch presents a flight-safety issue. If it does, that could delay certification of Boeing’s new 737 MAX 10 and complicate the entry into service of the recently approved MAX 7.

The software glitch can occur when a pilot needs to abort a landing attempt. The airplane’s autopilot is forced into a simpler level of automation for pitch control, which increases pilot workload compared to the standard mode used, the company said.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on the software glitch and its potential impact to Boeing’s certification schedule.

A permanent fix for the issue was originally slated for 2028, though the planemaker said it is working to accelerate that. In the meantime, a bulletin is being developed for pilots at 737 MAX operators.
14378151d7b070ac: JAKARTA: The death toll after a ferry sank in Indonesia's Java Sea almost two weeks ago has jumped to 64, an official said on Saturday, as rescuers extended the search for dozens still missing.

The Virgo Transport 8 was carrying 213 passengers and 30 crew when it lost contact with its shipping company after departing from Indonesia's second largest city Surabaya on Java island, headed for Banjarmasin on Borneo.
"Out of 243 persons onboard, 172 have been evacuated, 108 survived, 64 died, and 71 are still being searched for," National Search and Rescue Agency official Yudhi Bramantyo told a news conference.
Rescuers recovered four bodies from the submerged ship on Saturday, while seven others were found along the shoreline, Yudhi said.
He added that the search operation would be extended a further seven days but will be evaluated every three days.
Search-and-rescue operations typically last for seven days in Indonesia, and authorities can extend them based on factors including an assessment that some of the victims could still be recovered.
Marine accidents regularly occur in Indonesia, a vast Southeast Asian archipelago of more than 17,000 islands that relies heavily on boat connections for daily transport and tourism.
Lax safety standards and unpredictable weather are often the main reasons for disasters.
74b428711ad75cf2: NEW YORK: Malaysia mengulangi gesaan kuasa veto lima anggota tetap Majlis Keselamatan Pertubuhan Bangsa-bangsa Bersatu (UNSC) dimansuhkan kerana "muak" ia digunakan berulang kali untuk menggagalkan usaha mengambil tindakan terhadap isu Gaza.

Menteri Luar, Mohamad Hasan, berkata Malaysia dan negara anggota lain telah berusaha sedaya upaya menuntut keadilan untuk Gaza, termasuk gesaan melaksanakan gencatan senjata segera, bantuan kemanusiaan tanpa sekatan, tindakan punitif terhadap Israel serta keahlian penuh Palestin dalam PBB.

"Namun, berkali-kali kehendak kolektif perhimpunan ini disekat oleh kuasa veto. Malaysia ingin menyatakan secara terus-terang: Kami muak dengan keadaan ini," katanya ketika menyampaikan kenyataan negara pada sesi perbahasan umum Perhimpunan Agung PBB (UNGA) ke-81 di sini.

Mohamad berkata, keperluan melakukan pembaharuan paling kritikal dalam UNSC, di mana penggunaan kuasa veto mesti dipersoalkan dan dicabar sekeras-kerasnya oleh setiap anggota UNGA, khasnya dalam kes membabitkan jenayah terhadap kemanusiaan.
Jelasnya, Resolusi 76/262 yang diterima pakai pada 2022 telah mewujudkan saluran akauntabiliti antara UNSC dan UNGA.
"Kita mesti memanfaatkan sepenuhnya resolusi ini sebagai landasan ke arah akauntabiliti lebih besar berhubung penggunaan kuasa veto."
Tegasnya, memperluaskan keanggotaan UNSC semata-mata tidak memadai untuk menangani kelemahannya.
"Kuasa veto inilah yang mesti dicabar, dan kuasa veto inilah yang mesti dihapuskan. Kita mesti memulakan usaha ini sekarang."

Sebelum ini, Malaysia menggesa pemansuhan kuasa veto, di samping menyokong sekatan terhadap penggunaannya dalam kes membabitkan pelanggaran serius undang-undang antarabangsa, jika pemansuhan sepenuhnya tidak dapat dicapai.
Pada masa sama, Malaysia turut menyokong usaha memperluaskan jumlah anggota tetap dan tidak tetap UNSC untuk menjadikan badan itu lebih inklusif serta mewakili pelbagai pihak.

UNSC sering menemui jalan buntu dalam usaha mencapai gencatan senjata di Gaza, dengan Amerika Syarikat menggunakan kuasa veto menghalang beberapa resolusi, walaupun mendapat sokongan meluas anggota lain.

Pada Jun 2025, AS menggunakan kuasa veto terhadap draf resolusi menggesa gencatan senjata segera dan kekal di Gaza, walaupun 14 anggota lain menyokongnya. Washington sekali lagi menggunakan kuasa veto terhadap resolusi gencatan senjata Gaza sama pada September tahun lalu.

Mohamad dalam ucapan penutupnya berkata, PBB perlu melakukan pembaharuan terhadap institusi yang tidak lagi mencerminkan realiti semasa serta memastikan peraturan sistem global diguna pakai secara saksama kepada semua pihak.
Jelasnya, Malaysia terus berpegang kepada prinsip multilateralisme, "khasnya apabila pilihan lain ialah dunia yang dikuasai kuasa semata-mata".
"Malaysia tidak akan berpaling daripada PBB pada saat ia berdepan kesukaran.
"Kami tidak akan meninggalkan multilateralisme hanya kerana ia tidak sempurna. Kami akan berusaha untuk menjadikannya layak menerima kepercayaan."
5c5dbb32c6eef258: BUENOS AIRES: Hurricane Polo moved away from Mexico's Pacific coast on Saturday as a downgraded Category 4, before an expected return to make landfall in Baja California Sur on Monday, forecasters said.

On Saturday afternoon, Polo was about 531km south west of the Mexican resort town of Cabo San Lucas, with maximum sustained winds of 233 kph, according to the US National Hurricane Center. The storm was moving north west at 14 kph.
The NHC downgraded the hurricane from Category 5 on Saturday.

AccuWeather, a private ​forecaster, reported that Polo is expected to gradually lose intensity and hit Baja California as a Category 2. It's due to make landfall in an area away from dense population centres but with some small towns such as Las Barrancas, it said.

Twenty-four hours after landfall, the hurricane is expected to make a second landfall along the coast of mainland northwestern Mexico, bringing potential life-threatening flash flooding to parts of Baja California Sur, Sinaloa, Sonora and Chihuahua, AccuWeather reported.

The hurricane’s heavy rain and strong winds along Mexico’s Pacific coast forced evacuations, port closures and school cancellations this week. ​In the resort city of San Jose del Cabo, police officers restricted access to a beach on Friday as the hurricane generated high waves and dangerous surf conditions.
Hurricane conditions are possible on Monday afternoon from Punta Eugenia to Santa Fe in Baja California, the NHC said.

Polo is expected to dump 10-20 cm of rain across parts of Baja California Sur, with maximum amounts of 10 inches, which could produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, the NHC said. It could also cause life-threatening surf, rip currents and coastal flooding.

71a8aac21a94f4aa: WHEN Sean Gallagher stood before an audience in Kuala Lumpur recently to present Witness to a Changing Planet, stories from "the front lines of climate change, environmental loss and a world in transition", he wasn't simply showing photographs.

For almost 25 years, the British environmental photojournalist and filmmaker has been travelling to places where forests disappear, rivers are poisoned, deserts advance and communities find themselves living with the consequences of a changing planet.

His keynote at International Sustainability Week 2026, held at the Malaysia International Trade and Exhibition Centre, drew on those years of witnessing environmental change, from the Tibetan Plateau and drought-stricken India, to rising seas in Tuvalu. But the stories behind the photographs are, ultimately, about something much more intimate: people, and what happens to them when the places they call home begin to change.
It's a theme that has followed Gallagher since he was 22, long before climate change became the defining environmental conversation it is today.

That was when, as a young zoologist on a field trip in southern Brazil, he spent three weeks living at a field station deep in the Atlantic rainforest, helping to study and protect what remained of one of the world's most threatened forest ecosystems.

Gallagher carried little more than a point-and-shoot film camera with him. He'd arrived with the instincts of a scientist, observing the forest and trying to understand what was happening to it. But somewhere among the trees, he realised ed that understanding the science was only part of the story. He could see what was happening; what he struggled to convey was what it felt like to be there.

"I needed something else," recalls Gallagher, seated beside me after his compelling keynote, looking decidedly more polished than the rugged field photographer who's spent much of his career sleeping in remote communities and venturing into some of the world's most fragile landscapes.
Yet beneath the dark blue blazer and grey trousers, that same field-hardened curiosity remains — evident in the way he talks about the places he's seen and the people he has encountered.
That realisation would quietly change the course of his life.
BEYOND BEAUTIFUL PICTURES

Back in Britain, his mother gave him her old Canon film camera. Gallagher began teaching himself photography through library books and second-hand equipment, eventually building a darkroom at home where he'd stay up until two, three, sometimes four in the morning printing photographs after spending the day shooting.
He was hooked. What had begun as a way of expressing something science couldn't became a vocation: using photography to tell stories about what happens when human beings and the environment collide.

After an internship at Magnum Photos in London, Gallagher began to see how photography could move beyond beautiful pictures and become a way of telling stories about social, political and environmental change.

And he discovered something else about himself — that he loved the stories nobody was talking about. He'd look at a subject through the eyes of the zoologist he'd trained to be and wonder: Is anybody in the newspapers talking about this?
That question eventually took him to China.

In 2006, still young enough to take a chance on an unfamiliar country, Gallagher looked at a map and decided that China was somewhere people would want to know more about. It became home and his first major environmental project there focused on desertification — at a time when climate change and global warming were not yet the front-page subjects they are today.

He travelled thousands of kilometres through northern and western China, documenting the effects of desertification on landscapes and communities. The work was supported by the Pulitzer Centre, which backed his reporting on an environmental issue that was receiving comparatively little attention.

It was the beginning of a pattern that would come to define his career. If an environmental crisis was distant, poorly understood or easy to overlook, Gallagher wanted to go there. And once he arrived, he wanted to find the people inside the story.

Voice low, he shares: "I'm not a nature photographer. I live in that space between human society and the environment, where they clash." Perhaps that's why, after nearly two decades of photographing some of the world's most damaged environments, it's still the people he remembers most vividly.

He remembers the smell of a place, the sound of it, the light, the faces… A photograph, says Gallagher, is never simply an image to him; it's a doorway back into a moment. One of those moments came while he was documenting industrial pollution along the Ganges in northern India.

The leather industry there, explains Gallagher, stretches back to factories established during British rule, and decades of pollution have had devastating consequences for people living and farming around the river.

He met an older man, already in his 60s, whose wife had died as a result of pollution. At first, the man spoke with the stoicism Gallagher had encountered so often among people living through hardship. Then, as he talked about his wife and his family, something gave way.
"He just broke down," remembers Gallagher.
It's the sort of moment that stays with a photographer long after the camera has been put away. "Moments like that… this is why I do it," he adds softly. "To tell those stories."

For Gallagher, an environmental story cannot simply be about melting ice caps, burning forests or endangered animals viewed from a safe distance. The scale of the climate crisis can be so vast that it becomes almost impossible to grasp.
People, however, understand people.

A polluted river becomes something different when we see the family whose lives depend upon it. A disappearing forest becomes more than a statistic when we meet the people trying to protect it, or those whose lives have already been altered by its loss.

This is where Gallagher's empathy becomes central to his work. He's conscious of the uncomfortable privilege of being able to arrive in a community, photograph what's happening and eventually leave. But he no longer believes the world's environmental crises belong only to the people living closest to them.
"I don't think any of us get to walk away anymore, really," he says simply.
For the affable Englishman, that also means refusing to portray people simply as victims.

If there's suffering, he will photograph it. But he also wants to show dignity, resistance, adaptation and resilience — the ways people continue to find a way forward even when the circumstances around them are overwhelming.
LOOK CLOSER

That instinct runs through his work in Cambodia, where he documented deforestation and forest fires in Cambodia Burning. The story appealed to him partly because environmental destruction in Southeast Asia was receiving less international attention than similar crises elsewhere. But the way he told it was just as important as the story itself.

Rather than relying solely on conventional documentary narration, Gallagher worked with a young Cambodian poet, asking her to respond to the footage through her own feelings and words. When he saw the finished film, he cried.

It was another reminder that there's always a new way of reaching someone. Gallagher knows he has to keep finding them because these days, he's not simply competing with newspapers, magazines or television documentaries.
He's competing with everything that flickers across our screens, all day and every day: Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, the endless scroll on our phones.
In that noisy world, a photograph has only a moment to make us stop.

Perhaps we pause because something in the light catches us. Perhaps we want to know where it was taken, who that person is, what has happened to them. Gallagher hopes that moment of curiosity will lead somewhere — to a caption, a name, a search, or a story we might otherwise never have found.
For him, the photograph is never the end of the conversation — it's simply the door. And perhaps that's why he has never been afraid of beauty, even when photographing something difficult.

Gallagher says that a beautiful image can draw us towards places we might otherwise turn away from. The beauty isn't meant to soften the horror or make it easier to bear; it's what makes us look long enough to see it.
MODEST AMBITION

But after almost 25 years of following these stories into some of the world's most difficult places, Gallagher knows there's a price to being the one who keeps looking. There are days, he admits, when he wonders how much longer he can do it.

Assignments mean time away from his family. There have been years of travelling, sleeping in unfamiliar places, entering polluted environments and witnessing landscapes under extraordinary pressure. Sometimes, after returning to a hotel at the end of a long day, he looks through the photographs he has made and wonders why he keeps putting himself through it.
The answer, increasingly, is his children.

Gallagher has two young children, and when he thinks about the future, he doesn't imagine it in abstract terms. He wonders where they'll live, what their cities will look like, which places will still be safe and what problems they'll have to navigate when they're adults.

Those questions have become part of what drives him to keep reporting. He wants his children, one day, to look at his work and know that their father tried to do something positive with the skills he had.

It's a remarkably modest ambition for a man who has photographed presidents and prime ministers, slept in the homes of Tibetan nomads and travelled through deserts, forests and communities most people will never encounter.
But Gallagher doesn't believe photography will save the planet. He sees his work as something smaller, and perhaps more lasting. Evidence.

In 100 years, 200 years, 500 years, people may look back at this period and ask how the world changed, what happened to its forests and rivers, how communities lived through those changes and what people knew while it was happening.

Gallagher wants his photographs to be part of that record. Not simply evidence that he was there, but evidence of what was happening to people and places while the rest of the world was still trying to understand the scale of the transformation.
WAKE UP CALL

For someone who has spent much of his life documenting environmental destruction, Gallagher is, perhaps surprisingly, a hopeful man. He credits much of that outlook to his mother, a nurse and midwife who worked in different parts of the world and somehow remained positive through it all.
Perhaps she taught him to look beyond what's broken.

He has since found that same instinct in many of the people he's met while documenting a changing planet — the quiet determination to adapt, rebuild what they can and carry on, even when the world around them is shifting.
It's a quality Gallagher believes humanity will need more than ever as he's increasingly convinced that the climate crisis is no longer a problem waiting somewhere in the future. It's already here.

"We're going to blow past 1.5°C," he says, referring to the internationally recognised climate target, his frustration palpable at how slowly the world has responded despite decades of scientific warnings.

The difficulty, he adds, is that climate change rarely arrives with one dramatic moment that makes everyone stop and pay attention. Instead, it accumulates almost quietly — a little more heat, a little less water, another forest gone, another community displaced, another river polluted — until what once seemed distant is suddenly part of everyday life.
"It's here, it's now and it's serious."
WHAT WE CHOOSE TO DO

Perhaps that's why the camera remains so important to him. Gallagher describes it as another language, even a little passport, opening doors into places, cultures, families and communities he might otherwise never encounter.

Through the viewfinder, the world becomes a rectangle of light, geometry and possibility. He waits, watches, studies the frame and then, sometimes, everything falls into place. The moment is captured, and almost immediately he's looking for the next one.

His first paid photograph, incidentally, was a decidedly less glamorous affair: a picture of a local hotel for a newspaper, which he concedes was probably terrible. He earned about £10. More than two decades later, the thrill remains. Only now, the stories have become immeasurably larger.

When he's not on assignment, Gallagher rides. During the Covid-19 pandemic, he helped start a cycling club in Beijing that has since grown to more than 500 members. Earlier this year, he and a friend rode the length of the Great Wall, covering roughly 2,400km in nine days.

There's something of Gallagher in that restlessness — the need to keep moving and to see what lies beyond the next bend. Perhaps it's also what has carried him this far: not any illusion that he can fix everything he photographs, but the belief that there's value in bearing witness, telling the story and, above all, helping us understand one another.

For Gallagher, the camera began as a way of expressing what science couldn't. And nearly 25 years later, it has become something more. It's a way of crossing borders and differences, and of reminding us that the environmental crises we reduce to statistics are, in the end, lived by human beings.
The photographs may outlive him. He certainly hopes they will.

Long after he has stopped travelling to the places he has spent a lifetime documenting, perhaps they'll still be there, telling someone what happened: who was there, what they endured, how they adapted and what the world looked like when it was changing beneath their feet.
Because the stories Gallagher has spent his life telling aren't really about the end of the world. They're about the people living through it — and what we choose to do while there's still time.
