a21eafee2f5eb781: PETALING JAYA: PRN Melaka akan benar-benar menguji kemampuan parti-parti komponen Perikatan Nasional (PN) menarik sokongan pengundi tanpa identiti bersama, sekiranya lambang gabungan itu tidak boleh digunakan.
PN ketika ini dianggotai PAS, Wawasan, Gerakan, Parti Rakyat India Malaysia (MIPP) dan Parti Pejuang Tanah Air (Pejuang), serta Bersatu di sebalik persoalan mengenai kedudukannya.
Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri dari Global Asia Consulting percaya ketiadaan lambang PN boleh memberi kesan kepada penyelarasan kempen.
"Logo bukan sekadar lambang. Ia adalah identiti yang membantu pengundi mengenal siapa yang mereka undi dan gabungan yang diwakili," katanya kepada FMT.

JPPM dilaporkan menggantung semua kegiatan PN berkuat kuasa 23 Sept susulan aduan Bersatu, yang menurut setiausaha agung parti itu berkenaan pelanggaran perlembagaan PN oleh kepimpinan baharu gabungan itu.
JPPM berkata, penggantungan itu bertujuan menjaga kepentingan pertubuhan dan mencegah PN daripada terus melanggar peraturannya.

Awang Azman Awang Pawi dari Universiti Malaya percaya penggantungan itu boleh menjejaskan momentum PN dari segi organisasi, penjenamaan dan persepsi mengenai kesatuan gabungan itu, terutama jika parti komponen menggunakan lambang masing-masing.
"Ini boleh menyebabkan mesej gabungan menjadi kurang jelas," katanya kepada FMT.

Awang Azman bagaimanapun berkata keadaan PN "yang tidak menentu" tidak boleh dianggap sebagai memberi kelebihan kepada Pakatan Harapan (PH), kerana keputusan pilihan raya bergantung kepada calon, jentera, isu tempatan dan kemamppuan memindahkan sokongan antara parti.
"Cabaran sebenar ialah soal identiti pilihan raya. Kekuatan mereka masih bergantung kepada calon, jentera, isu tempatan dan kemampuan memindahkan sokongan antara parti," katanya.
Di sebalik perkembangan ini, Zaharuddin berkata Bersatu kini berdepan persoalan dengan mengenai hala tuju.

"Jika tidak mahu BN dan hubungan dengan PAS pula retak, ke mana Bersatu hendak pergi? Itu persoalan yang paling tajam sekarang. Bersatu perlu menentukan sama ada mahu mempertahankan kerjasama sedia ada atau mencari laluan baharu," katanya.
Awang Azman percaya PRN Melaka berpotensi menguji tiga model kerjasama politik, iaitu BN+, PH+ dan penyusunan semula parti-parti komponen PN.
900a3b563033235f: ALOR GAJAH: For many people, a durian orchard visit is simple enough - wait for the fruit to fall, crack it open and eat.
At one orchard in Alor Gajah, however, visitors can also get a closer look at how the trees are grown, how different varieties behave, and even how two types of durian can share the same tree.
Managed by Duta Riang Villa, which opened last year, the orchard spans about 17ha and contains some 1,600 durian trees, including Musang King, Black Thorn, Kim Hong and Udang Merah.
Koh Kai Xiang, who runs the site, said the idea was to give visitors more than a quick tasting session, especially beyond the main durian season.
Alongside the orchard are recreational activities such as a mini zoo, archery and ATV rides, giving families more reasons to linger rather than simply turn up for fruit and leave.

Still, the durians themselves remain at the heart of the experience. Visitors can learn how to identify different varieties, what affects fruit quality and how durian trees are cared for as they move from flowering to fruit development.

That can be surprisingly complex. Orchard worker Ahmad Safwan Fathi Zainuddin said different varieties do not mature at the same rate, with Musang King and Udang Merah typically falling earlier than Black Thorn.
Care also changes according to weather and the stage of growth, from flowering and fruit-setting to the period when the fruit is developing.
One of the more unusual sights in the orchard is a grafted tree carrying two varieties at once.
“It is the same tree, with Kim Hong at the bottom and Musang King at the top,” Ahmad Safwan pointed out.
Both grow from the same root system, with one variety grafted onto another part of the tree. According to him, the combination may also produce larger fruit compared with some ordinary trees.
The fruit itself can vary in appearance, too. Musang King, for example, is not always perfectly round and can sometimes grow in a more elongated shape.
Details like these are part of what Koh hopes visitors take away from an orchard trip: a better sense of how much work happens before a durian ever reaches the table.
The Melaka durian season usually peaks from May to July, although the timing can shift depending on weather and growing conditions.
Some visitors return the following season after learning more about the fruit, Koh noted, while the orchard has also attracted tourists from overseas including South Korea.

For those accustomed to seeing durian mainly at roadside stalls or in boxes, walking among the trees here offers a different perspective - one where the fruit is not just something to eat, but something to understand.
24b763f23e794b8a: The mood on the ground in Malaysia is heavy with a deep, suffocating weariness. People are simply tired
They are tired of politics and the power plays that have dragged focus, energy and resources away from building the economy and addressing the rising cost of living.

They are tired of watching the federal unity government navigate its own fragile choreography—with Umno Youth rattling sabres about realignments with PAS, whispers of possible early polls and convicted former prime minister Najib Razak’s conditional royal pardon which allows for house arrest.

Adding to the turbulence, the Negeri Sembilan political landscape appears to be spinning into administrative chaos. What began as a move by several traditional chieftains (undang) to remove the ruler has become more entangled and ugly with the involvement of the menteri besar and state executive council in a high-stakes power play.
The people are exhausted by a system where political survival and power are chased for their own sake, while ordinary families bear the brunt of rising costs and uneven development.

Compounding this instability is something even more dangerous: a profound crisis of public trust. Malaysians have grown deeply cynical, widely viewing politicians as power-hungry actors looking out primarily for themselves.
How do we break out of this exhausting loop? Perhaps the answer lies not in inventing new political spin, but in turning back the clock to timeless wisdom.

Global leaders occasionally lean on ancient texts to remind modern states of foundational statecraft. This was brought sharply into focus when reports emerged of India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi presenting Russian President Vladimir Putin with a Russian translation of the ancient Thirukkural on the sidelines of the recent BRICS summit in New Delhi.
Having read the text, I could understand Modi's choice of cultural diplomacy—taking a 2,000-year-old masterpiece on governance, ethics, and human conduct and placing it on the global stage.

Modi frequently quotes from the Thirukkural, as does our own Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. For instance, in tabling the 2024 federal budget in October 2023, Anwar noted that according to the Thirukkural, a good ruler is one who is capable of creating wealth, acquiring it, protecting it, and distributing it wisely for the welfare of the people.
In 2025, in talking about the burdens of the rising cost of living in Parliament, Anwar reminded Malaysians of the text's lesson that steadfastness of the heart is a core mark of human virtue.

Long before modern party politics and coalition arithmetic, the ancient Tamil text—composed by Tiruvalluvar—laid down a remarkably clear framework for governance. Its core principles offer an unsparing mirror for today’s politicians if they care to look.

Early icons of independent Malaysia understood this resonance. First prime minister Tunku Abdul Rahman heaped profuse praise upon the Thirukkural, as did national laureate Dr Ismail Hussein, who felt it held vital lessons for all of mankind.

Perhaps it’s time to introduce today’s politicians to this timeless wisdom, which transcends race, religion, and creed. We already possess distinguished Malay translations of the Tamil original, including works by Dr Ismail Hussein and Dr S Singaravelu, formerly of Universiti Malaya.

If our members of Parliament and state assemblymen genuinely imbibe these tenets, our public life could look entirely different, providing an ethical counterweight against systemic governance failures.
The Thirukkural rests on three essential pillars: aram (justice/virtue/righteousness), porul (material prosperity/politics/governance) and inbam (love/joy/human connection).

Aram deals with ethics, morality, and the leading of a balanced, honest life; porul focuses on the practicalities of governance, economics, and the social responsibilities of citizens and leaders; and inbam explores the nuances of intimacy, longing, and emotional connection.

The Thirukkural has many gems for both the ordinary citizen and rulers/leaders. For instance, it says good rulers/leaders are marked by courage, liberality, wisdom, energy, diligence and learning. They must also be easy of access and soft-spoken.

At the heart of the text with 1,330 couplets or Kural is a deep commitment to justice, the virtue that prevents resentment and division. Tiruvalluvar insists that true leaders must act with strict impartiality and safeguard the dignity of every single citizen.

In today's climate of fragile state-level realignments and casual ethnic grandstanding, this is more urgent than ever. Kural 317, for instance, states: "It is the highest wisdom not to cause pain to any living creature, at any time, in any degree, even in thought."

For our leaders, this is a practical warning against the abuse of power and divisive rhetoric that leaves communities feeling marginalised. Applying justice means defending an independent judiciary, maintaining fearless anti-corruption frameworks, and enacting policies rooted in equal opportunity rather than racial patronage.
Equally critical is the text’s emphasis on economic pragmatism and resource management, prioritising public welfare over elite accumulation.
For instance, Kural 385 says: "To acquire wealth, store it up, guard it, and distribute it wisely—these are the four distinct marks of an accomplished ruler (government)."

In practical terms, this means our leaders must stop treating national development projects as tools for cronyism or personal enrichment. Tax collected must be used for public benefit and every ringgit spent must be designed to uplift the people equitably.

The text places supreme importance on moral character and ethical duty. Leadership is not about bare political survival or relentless power plays; it is about steadfast integrity. As Kural 954 notes: “Even if wealth piled high is offered, those of good family will not do anything that lowers their honour.”
In a political culture scarred by broken promises, patronage politics, abuse of government resources and corruption, this is the missing link.

Ultimately, the Thirukkural is more than an ancient classic; it is a reality check for modern Malaysia. It reminds us that a nation’s true wealth is measured not by towering skyscrapers or quarterly GDP figures, but by the safety and dignity of its humblest citizen.
If our leaders have the courage to choose principled, people-centred governance over tactical survival, they - and we citizens - will find that Malaysia’s greatest days are still ahead.

39ce43c28c308777: IT'S barely 7.30am when members of Wira Transplant Malaysia begin arriving at a little park in Taman Melawati, opposite the MPAJ Melawati Convention Centre, carrying buntings and signage for their morning walk.

The patch of green sits almost unnoticed between buildings, the sort of neighbourhood park you could easily pass without a second glance. As the neighbourhood slowly wakes, so does this gathering of transplant recipients, dialysis patients, doctors, caregivers and supporters, many greeting one another with the easy familiarity of old friends.
Before anyone starts walking, the group warms up together, stretching arms, rolling shoulders and bending knees, with laughter whenever someone misses a movement.
Nobody is expected to move faster than they comfortably can.

There's learning too. Dr Nurul Zaynah Nordin, a nephrologist at Kuala Lumpur Hospital, gives a talk on kidney care, explaining chronic kidney disease (CKD), its risk factors and why Malaysians need to pay attention to their kidney health.

"Chronic kidney disease is a hidden burden," she shares, pointing to diabetes, hypertension and obesity as important risk factors. By stage five, patients will usually require some form of kidney replacement therapy and, for suitable patients, transplantation offers the best chance of moving away from long-term dialysis.

When the group eventually sets off, they walk gently around the park, chatting and welcoming curious passers-by who stop to find out what's happening. From a distance, there's nothing remarkable about the sight. But spend a little time among them and those ordinary steps begin to mean something else.

For someone whose week is organised around dialysis sessions, a morning walking freely in a park can mean far more than exercise. For a transplant recipient, every step is also possible because somebody, somewhere, gave.

And that, in many ways, explains what Wira Transplant is about. The patient-led non-profit group grew from a desire to bring together people whose lives have been touched by organ failure and transplantation, from recipients and those still waiting for organs to dialysis patients, caregivers and the medical professionals who care for them.

It has developed into both a support network and an advocacy group, creating opportunities for patients to meet, share experiences and remain active while raising public awareness about organ donation. Wira also gives patients a collective voice on the challenges they face, including access to transplantation and improvements they believe are needed within Malaysia's transplant system.
A COMMUNITY TAKES SHAPE
Wira Transplant Malaysia president Manvir Victor knows that journey from the inside. Long before he became an advocate, he was a patient trying to build a life around kidney failure.
"I was diagnosed with end-stage renal failure in 2001 and went on dialysis soon after. I was on dialysis for 10 years and it was extremely difficult," he recalls.
Then came the gift that would change his life, when the woman he'd met and married became his kidney donor.
"I had my transplant in 2012 after my wife decided to donate a kidney to me," says Manvir.
The transplant gave him a new life, but it also opened his eyes to difficulties that didn't necessarily disappear with a functioning kidney.
"After a transplant, some patients suddenly find they cannot get a job because employers still classify them as sick."
It was a perception he wanted to challenge. In 2022, on the 10th anniversary of his transplant, friends from the Rotary Club of Melawati suggested climbing Mount Kinabalu.

Manvir initially hesitated, but the idea soon took on a larger purpose: if transplant recipients could take on one of the country's toughest physical challenges, perhaps people would begin to see what they were capable of rather than simply seeing them as patients.

About 20 people made that first climb, including three transplant recipients. The following year came the first Transplant Walk at Taman Tasik Titiwangsa, an accessible 3km route bringing doctors, transplant recipients and dialysis patients together. The walks eventually expanded to other parts of the country, creating the kind of community I see around me this morning.
"Don't look at the disease. Look at the person," urges Manvir, adding: "Wira means hero, but the heroes are not us. They're the donors, doctors and nurses who make transplants possible."
LIVING WHILE WAITING

There's something wonderfully defiant about Leelavathi K. Raju. At 49, she has already known the freedom a new kidney can bring, the heartbreak of losing it 15 years later and, now, the uncertainty of waiting for another.
"I received my first transplant in 2006 after about seven or eight months on dialysis. It lasted about 15 years before I had to go back on dialysis in August 2021," she shares.
Five years later, she's still waiting, but there's nothing passive about the way she waits.

"On dialysis days, I keep it simple with a 3km walk. On non-dialysis days, I go to the gym," she says blithely. "In May, I climbed the stairs of the 118-storey Merdeka 118 and completed the challenge in 53 minutes. Two days later, after dialysis, I flew to Kota Kinabalu and climbed Mount Kinabalu."
Her strength doesn't make the waiting any easier. Shares Leelavathi: "It has been five years and I'm still waiting. The best donation is organ donation because you're giving someone hope."
Sitting at the other end of that waiting game is Jishnu Gunalan, just 20 and finally able to think about the ordinary things young people his age take for granted: work, college and what comes next.
He was only 5 when doctors discovered he had stage three renal failure, beginning a childhood shaped by medication and eventually continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD).

"I was on CAPD for about seven years before I switched to haemodialysis," shares Jishnu. That continued for another five to six years until July 27 last year, when he finally received a kidney transplant.
"I was scared, but I was also happy and grateful," he recalls.

Today, Jishnu works at a cinema and is preparing to begin a diploma in business administration. Perhaps the most telling thing he says is also the simplest: "People see me as normal now and life is going great. It gives people like me a second life and a chance to have a future."
THE CALL THAT CHANGED EVERYTHING

Siti Rahayu Abdullah wasn't among the walkers that morning, but listening to her later, I find myself thinking again about those simple laps around the park and how easily the rest of us take such freedom for granted.

The 36-year-old Orang Asli woman was around 20 when lupus nephritis caused her kidneys to fail. She became so weak that after returning from work, she sometimes had to stop on the stairs because she simply couldn't make it to her fourth-floor home.
Eventually she collapsed and was hospitalised, waking from a coma to a life that would now revolve around dialysis.
Years of treatment followed before she began receiving calls about possible donor kidneys.
"The first time I was called, I was very anxious and scared because I'd never experienced anything like it," she recalls.
After several calls and disappointments, her chance finally came in October 2023. Siti Rahayu later discovered that her donor had been a 66-year-old Chinese woman.
"I was just happy. It didn't matter to me whether my donor was Chinese, Indian or from any other community. Whoever it was, I was grateful," she says.
She once asked whether she could meet the donor's family but was advised that donor and recipient identities were confidential.
"I would say terima kasih tak terhingga (thank you beyond words), especially to the family for allowing their loved one's wish to donate to be fulfilled."

Today, her definition of freedom is strikingly simple. Says Siti Rahayu: "I'm free from dialysis three times a week and from having needles in my arm. I can drink more water and I have more freedom to do other things. That freedom makes me happy."
GIFT BEYOND GRIEF
But every second chance has another story behind it, and sometimes it belongs to a family who had to say yes on the worst day of their lives.

For Bazli Yahya, that day came when his 31-year-old son, Muhammad Syukri Bazli, a cook, husband and father, developed an unbearable headache and deteriorated with frightening speed. Within days, he was in intensive care.
It was there that doctors approached the family about organ donation while they were still struggling to comprehend that Syukri might not survive.

Recalls Bazli: "My feelings were all mixed up because we still didn't know whether our son was going to survive. The doctors explained how his organs could help other people, but there was no pressure. They gave us time to think about it."
Bazli searched for information and discussed it with his wife and Syukri's widow.
"After two days, Alhamdulillah (praise be to God), our hearts were opened and we agreed to donate his organs, at least to help somebody."
Syukri's organs went on to help three people, including two teenagers.
"No words can describe how we felt when we knew his organs could help other people. We felt very blessed," says Bazli.

Before Syukri was taken from the ICU to the operating theatre for the donation procedure, hospital staff gave him a Walk of Honour, accompanying him on that final journey, a gesture Bazli says had given the family strength.

Syukri may be gone, but his father's advocacy hasn't stopped. Even his son's Proton Satria now carries organ-donation awareness stickers, a small, moving reminder of the decision the family made when grief was still unbearably raw.
Asked how he hopes his son will be remembered, Bazli doesn't hesitate. "I hope people will remember him as a pahlawan (hero)."
MANY WHEELS, ONE LIFE

Syukri's gift also reveals something easily forgotten when we talk about organ donation: saying yes is only the beginning. Once an organ becomes available, an extraordinary chain of people and processes has to move, often against the clock.

"A transplant depends on an entire ecosystem," explains Dr Vijayan Manogran, consultant neurologist at Columbia Asia Hospital Setapak and visiting transplant surgeon at Kuala Lumpur Hospital, Prince Court Medical Centre and Sunway Medical Centre.
"There are many wheels moving in transplantation and all of them have to move together," he adds.
Those wheels include doctors, surgeons, anaesthetists, donor coordinators, procurement teams and transplant teams.

It is why Wira's advocacy goes beyond persuading more Malaysians to become organ donors. A donated organ represents an extraordinary gift, but Manvir argues that the system must be ready to honour that gift.

Increasing donor numbers, he believes, must go hand in hand with stronger national coordination, sufficient expertise and resources and, ultimately, a dedicated transplant institute capable of bringing the different parts of that ecosystem together.
For the person waiting at the other end, these are not abstract questions of infrastructure. They can determine whether that long-awaited second chance actually comes.

Dr Nurul, meanwhile, wants people to understand just how far one act of donation can reach. She says: "One deceased donor can save at least eight lives. When two kidneys are donated, two patients can potentially be freed from dialysis."
Dr Vijayan brings it back to the human being waiting at the other end.
"You can make a difference to somebody's life. You can give them a second chance," he says.
EVERY STEP COUNTS

By the time the walkers make their final rounds in Taman Melawati, the morning has grown warmer. Dr Nurul's kidney-care talk is over, the exercises are done and conversations have been struck up with strangers who stopped simply because they were curious.

Soon, the buntings and signage will be packed away, but the realities they came here to talk about will continue. Leelavathi will return to dialysis while waiting for another kidney, Jishnu can look towards college after spending much of his childhood around treatment and Siti Rahayu will continue living with a kidney given by a woman she never knew.
Three other people have more time with those they love because, at the most painful moment of his family's life, Syukri became a donor.
a66fc0ea7f093492: NEW YORK: Malaysia has called for greater involvement of Global South countries in global discussions on artificial intelligence (AI).

Foreign minister Mohamad Hasan said AI was transforming economies, societies and the way governments made decisions, while a small number of private actors now controlled how billions of people communicated, worked, transacted and consumed information.
He reminded that technology “must serve humanity, never the reverse”, warning that a small number of companies or countries should not be allowed to decide the rules for everyone else.

“The Global South cannot simply become a destination for data centres while decisions about AI are made elsewhere,” he said when delivering Malaysia’s national statement at the general debate of the 81st UN General Assembly here today.
“We must be partners in innovation. Not merely customers and markets. And not merely destinations for investment.”

Mohamad added that equitable decision-making and development also meant managing the enormous demands created by technological infrastructure, including its use of water, energy, land and other resources.
He said this was necessary to ensure the benefits of AI could be shared more broadly across borders.
The call comes as the UN steps up efforts to develop a global approach to AI governance, with the first session of its Global Dialogue on AI Governance held in Geneva in July.
The initiative is intended to provide an inclusive platform for countries to discuss the opportunities and risks posed by AI.
The issue is also particularly relevant to Malaysia, which has positioned itself as a regional hub for data centres and AI infrastructure.

Separately, Mohamad urged parties involved in the escalating conflict in West Asia to step back, warning that disruption to the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, both critical routes for global energy and trade, would have consequences beyond the region.
"A family in Southeast Asia has no part in these disputes. Yet that family still pays the price when food, fuel, and cost of living rise."
He said middle powers such as Malaysia, along with regional organisations such as Asean, could help keep dialogue alive when major powers could not agree.
“We must have the confidence to speak for our regions, not be spoken for,” he said.

034d841d17abf361: STRENGTHENING the nation's food security involves not only producing more food, but also building a resilient domestic agricultural ecosystem that can sustain farmers and domestic supply over the long term.
In the padi fields of Kedah and Perlis, a partnership involving some 200 farmers is showing how stronger links between agriculture and domestic manufacturing can contribute to that effort.
Through the Nestle Paddy Club (NPC), farmers cultivate more than 600ha of padi.
Since 2012, 100 per cent of the white rice used in Nestle's Cerelac infant cereals, produced in Malaysia, has been sourced domestically.
The programme is expected to supply about 2,800 tonnes of rice this year.
Nestle (Malaysia) Bhd chief executive officer Juan Aranols said the programme reflected the company's focus on ingredient quality and its partnership with Malaysia's farming communities.

"Cerelac is an important brand because it is part of the nutrition we provide for babies aged 6 to 12 months. We apply all necessary care and quality requirements to ensure only the best ingredients go into the product.
"Rice is an important ingredient. We are here in the rice bowl of Malaysia, so we are proud to be partners with the local authorities and farming community," he said.
Beyond securing high-quality domestically grown rice, the programme also supports farmers to improve the way they farm.
NPC farmers get agricultural inputs every planting season, alongside knowledge and training, technical guidance in the field and support to improve crop quality.
The programme connects the rice they produce to Nestle's domestic manufacturing value chain. Participating farmers have consistently recorded yields above the national average.
For participant Bahriza Rejab, aged 53, the programme has changed the way he manages his crops.
"I'm a full-time padi farmer and have been in the industry for 30 years... The rice we produce is used to make baby food, so we don't want to use chemical pesticides.

"Nestle provides us with organic products from the time we sow the seeds until harvest. I'm fortunate because it provides them for free. The company also guide us in managing our crops to ensure that the rice we produce meets the requirements for baby food."
Fellow NPC farmer Sabri Nayan, 59, said the programme has encouraged more environmentally conscious farming practices.
"When we work with Nestle, we are taught and guided to care for the environment. When we use pesticides, we do not use just any product.

"The vitamins they provide are of high quality, and the silica helps strengthen the roots and support healthy growth. When the stems are stronger, the plants are more resistant to disease, resulting in healthier padi crops."
FROM FARM RESILIENCE TO FOOD SECURITY
The focus is now shifting towards making farming more resilient.
Healthier soils, more efficient farming practices and stronger farmer capabilities can help sustain yields, reduce production risks and better withstand climate and cost pressures.
In turn, this supports a more dependable domestic food supply.

A regenerative agriculture project for NPC farmers commenced in June, focusing on improving soil health, using water more efficiently, optimising agricultural inputs and reducing greenhouse gas emissions from rice cultivation.
The programme is also promoting practices such as Semi-Aerobic Rice Intensification and alternate wetting and drying.
KEEPING THE VALUE CHAIN LOCAL
After harvest, rice produced by NPC farmers is processed locally through milling, quality testing and manufacturing.
The process includes mechanical drying, storage, de-husking and several stages of polishing.
Rice samples undergo contaminant testing, microbiological analysis and chemical analysis to ensure they meet stringent quality and food safety requirements for infant nutrition.
Traceability is maintained throughout the journey from farm to finished product.

For farmers, this creates a direct link between what is grown in the fields of Kedah and Perlis and a domestically manufactured food product, while helping to build a reliable domestic supply of a key agricultural ingredient.
Padi is also part of Nestle Malaysia's wider domestic agricultural sourcing efforts under its Farmer Connect initiatives, which extend to chilli, coffee and cocoa.
For the NPC farmers, the benefits are felt on the ground: better crops, stronger livelihoods and the ability to continue farming from one season to the next.

5724e96a7b80b5cc: LOURDES, France: Pope Leo XIV prayed for France on Saturday at its holy shrine in Lourdes, after riding along the Champs Elysees in the popemobile and holding an emotional open-air mass in front of hundreds of thousands of worshippers in Paris.
The leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics is on a four-day trip to France, a secular country with deep Catholic roots, on the first official papal visit there in nearly two decades.
In the southwestern pilgrimage town the US pontiff prayed at the Grotto of Massabielle, where Catholic tradition holds that the Virgin Mary appeared in 1858 to a peasant girl, later Saint Bernadette.

Months of ahead of a presidential election with the far-right surging and immigration high on the agenda, he prayed to the Virgin Mary to "obtain for France wise and generous leaders... eager to serve the common good."
"May they make her (France's) voice heard in promoting the defence of fundamental human rights and peace in the world, rejecting the mentality of war once and for all."
AFP reporters saw him perform the rituals observed by the many pilgrims to the cave: touching the rock, lighting a candle and drinking spring water.

On Sunday, Leo will meet privately with seven victims of clerical sex abuse. A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as minors in France, over seven decades.
GIANT PARIS MASS

In an earlier highlight of the visit's second day, the 71-year-old pope led enthusiastic worshippers in a mass at Paris's Place de la Concorde, where a giant white canopy had been erected to serve as a makeshift altar.
His prayers were accompanied by choral and organ music as the sun broke through the grey skies.
"It is truly good and pleasant when brothers and sisters come together and glorify the greatness of God," said Pope Leo, dressed in white liturgical vestments.
Some 800,000 people had gathered all the way beyond the Arc de Triomphe, the Vatican said.
"It's one time in history to see the pope," said Aline Riziki, 41, who was born in the Democratic Republic of Congo and has lived in France for 11 years.
"I dropped everything to come here and see him, to pray for peace in the east" of her homeland, wracked by conflict for decades, she said.
'IMPORTANT MOMENT'
Jeanne de Montagnac, 29, came with her husband and two-year-old girl, who was perched on his shoulders.
"We're happy that, even if she won't remember it, we're sharing this with her," she said, a small golden cross dangling over her jumper.
"It's an important moment for us to be surrounded by other people who also have faith."
The first US pontiff was visiting France seven months before voters choose a successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron.
A number of presidential hopefuls were present, including far-right leader Marine Le Pen and centrist Edouard Philippe.

Macron did not attend the mass but was represented by his wife Brigitte. The president said in a message on X that France was "proud to welcome Pope Leo XIV and this monumental mass in the heart of Paris."
'DIGNITY AND PEACE'
Earlier in the day, the pope met migrants at Maison Bakhita, an association supporting refugees. Leo said it was "possible to encounter one another and to live together in dignity and peace."
He also stressed the "fundamental role of women in building a civilisation of love."
The association said the pope's visit sent a "message" ahead of the April-May election.
Leo was the third pope to visit Lourdes after Benedict XVI in 2008 and Jean-Paul II in 1983 and 2004.
Thousands of faithful watched his arrival at the site on giant screens.
The sanctuary, one of the most important Catholic holy sites in the world, receives some three million pilgrims each year. Catholics credit it with miraculous healings.

3e90d974f9221dd5: AT 7.15 on a weekday morning, the neighbourhood is already awake.

Schoolchildren are hustled into cars, somebody reverses a Myvi out of a porch with the skill of driving into a Formula One pit stop backwards, and the elderly pak cik two doors down is still watering plants in his sarong.
Somewhere, a gate clangs shut, a motorbike starts and someone calls out a hearty "Morning!"

It's an ordinary Malaysian day, the sort most of us barely notice. Yet there's something rather reassuring about the familiar choreography of people who live close enough to know one another's routines, even if they don't necessarily know one another very well.

We know which houses have children, who leaves for work before sunrise and when the house in the next lane is suddenly filling up with relatives because there's a wedding, kenduri or family gathering.
Increasingly, of course, we also know because someone has put it in the neighbourhood WhatsApp group.
This is why National Good Neighbour Day, celebrated in the United States on Sept 28, makes for an interesting import here.

The observance is American in origin. It was created in the early 1970s by Becky Mattson of Lakeside, Montana, before president Jimmy Carter issued a proclamation recognising National Good Neighbour Day in 1978.
It was originally observed on the 4th Sunday of September before the date was fixed as Sept 28 in 2003.
America, in other words, has a day to remind people to be good neighbours. Malaysia, meanwhile, has its own Rukun Tetangga.
MALAYSIAN NEIGHBOURLINESS
Launched on Aug 29, 1975, in Kampung Kasipillay, Kuala Lumpur, the scheme began primarily as a neighbourhood security initiative, with residents taking part in patrols.
Its role subsequently evolved to focus more broadly on neighbourliness, community development and local unity.
And if Rukun Tetangga is the machinery of Malaysian neighbourliness, perhaps Rukun Negara is its moral compass.
Proclaimed on Aug 31, 1970, in the aftermath of the events of May 13, 1969, Rukun Negara was introduced with the central objective of fostering stronger unity among Malaysians.

Its five principles are familiar to anyone who survived school assemblies and civic lessons: Belief in God; Loyalty to King and Country; Supremacy of the Constitution; Rule of Law; and, Courtesy and Morality.
That last one, Courtesy and Morality (Kesopanan dan Kesusilaan), is particularly useful when living as neighbours... because Malaysian neighbourliness comes with its own peculiar customs.

A good neighbour accepts your parcel when you're stuck in traffic and doesn't mind when you only manage to collect it at 10pm, although there's a reasonable chance the parcel has by then become a topic of conversation.
A good neighbour waters your plants while you balik kampung, feeds the cat if you ask nicely and, in a genuine emergency, may even have a spare key to your house.
And then there's food.

A neighbour who sends over a container of curry, rendang, kuih or freshly fried cucur isn't merely sharing food; they're establishing diplomatic relations, which is why returning that container empty is, in Malaysian terms, almost an act of aggression.
As my mother always insists: "Jangan bagi balik kosong! (Don't return it empty!)
Suffice to say, the rules aren't written anywhere — but everyone seems to know them.
BUILDING CONNECTIONS

Neighbours can become accidental members of our extended families: the kind auntie who notices when your child hasn't come home, the smiling uncle who knows a plumber who can fix your leaking pipe, or the family you barely knew until a death, wedding or flood brought everyone together.

And then there's the neighbourhood WhatsApp group, that uniquely modern institution which has somehow turned the simple business of living next to one another into a community noticeboard, lost-and-found counter, security alert system and occasional courtroom.
Anyone lost a cat?
Whose car is this?
Please don't throw rubbish here.
Water supply disruption tomorrow.
Watch out for the monkeys!
Then comes the inevitable photograph of a suspicious-looking individual, accompanied by a plea for everyone to be vigilant.
It can all be a little much, but beneath the neighbourhood gossip and parking disputes is something rather comforting: the knowledge that someone is paying attention.

That matters in an age when it is entirely possible to live in a condominium for five years and still not know the person across the corridor. We can be surrounded by people and remain strangers to them.

Perhaps that is why the idea behind National Good Neighbour Day resonates. Its organisers encourage people to meet those living closest to them, build connections and create a greater sense of belonging.
We don't have to become best friends with everyone on our street. That may be asking a little too much.
A good neighbour doesn't need to know your entire family history, your children's exam results or why you came home at 2am last Saturday.

Sometimes, "Kesopanan dan Kesusilaan" is simply knowing when to turn the music down, moving your car when it's blocking someone else's gate, returning the borrowed container and not treating the common drain as your personal rubbish bin.
It's also knowing when to knock on the door with a plate of something you've cooked and say, "I made too much."
Of course, we know that's not true. I mean, nobody makes that much sambal by accident!
Perhaps that's the real beauty of neighbourhoods. We don't choose the people who live next door to us.
They arrive with their barking dogs, noisy renovations, children, durians, cars, curry puffs, complaints and Christmas decorations, and, somehow, we learn to accommodate one another.
So, on Sept 28, while Americans celebrate National Good Neighbour Day, perhaps Malaysians can simply do what we've been doing in our own way for generations.
Say "hello" to the neighbour whose name you've never bothered to learn, or share that kuih you made on a whim.
How about checking on the elderly couple two doors down who might welcome a friendly "apa khabar"?
Or, if you're feeling particularly brave, introduce yourself properly in the neighbourhood WhatsApp group. You never know; you might even find a fellow pickleball kaki there.
Just remember one thing though. If you borrow the neighbour's container, don't forget to return it with something inside!

9d968d330667c1b5: PETALING JAYA: Pengerusi Jawatankuasa Undang-undang Jenayah Majlis Peguam Vivek Sukumaran mencadangkan beberapa langkah bagi mengurangkan kelewatan kes jenayah, termasuk memastikan siasatan utama hampir selesai sebelum seseorang didakwa.
Vivek berkata laporan kimia dan forensik sepatutnya sudah tersedia sebelum pertuduhan dibuat kerana siasatan yang belum lengkap boleh menyebabkan kes lambat dibawa ke perbicaraan.

Beliau turut mencadangkan kes membabitkan tertuduh yang masih dalam tahanan diberi keutamaan, selain kawalan lebih ketat terhadap penangguhan kes dan semakan kehakiman secara berkala bagi menentukan sama ada penahanan berterusan masih berasas.

Menurutnya, jumlah jaminan juga perlu ditetapkan berdasarkan kemampuan tertuduh kerana ada individu terus ditahan reman bagi kesalahan ringan hanya kerana tidak mampu membayar jaminan atau mendapatkan penjamin.
“Tiada orang patut ditahan lebih dua tahun tanpa keputusan mahkamah kecuali hakim berpuas hati ada alasan kukuh untuk berbuat demikian,” katanya kepada FMT.
Vivek mengulas laporan FMT mengenai kebimbangan Ketua Hakim Negara Wan Ahmad Farid Wan Salleh terhadap tertuduh yang ditahan reman terlalu lama sementara menunggu perbicaraan.

Beliau berkata had tempoh yang ditetapkan melalui undang-undang diperlukan bagi mengelakkan tertuduh terus berada dalam tahanan terlalu lama sebelum kes dibicarakan, selain memastikan kelewatan tidak menjejaskan prinsip seseorang dianggap tidak bersalah sehingga dibuktikan sebaliknya.

Walaupun pekeliling pendaftar pada 2017 menetapkan tempoh 12 bulan untuk menyelesaikan kes jenayah di Mahkamah Sesyen dan Majistret, dikira dari tarikh kes didaftarkan, tiada undang-undang yang mewajibkan seseorang tertuduh dibebaskan sekiranya perbicaraan tidak dimulakan dengan segera.
Vivek berkata keadaan itu bermakna seseorang tertuduh boleh kekal dalam tahanan selama bertahun-tahun selepas didakwa sementara menunggu perbicaraan.
Katanya, Malaysia boleh mencontohi England dan Wales yang menetapkan had tempoh tahanan melalui undang-undang, dengan lanjutan hanya dibenarkan mahkamah dalam keadaan luar biasa.

Scotland juga menetapkan had masa melalui undang-undang bagi prosiding jenayah membabitkan tertuduh dalam tahanan. Kegagalan mematuhi tempoh itu boleh menyebabkan tertuduh dibenarkan ikat jamin kecuali mahkamah meluluskan lanjutan.
Vivek berkata Malaysia juga boleh membenarkan lanjutan tempoh jika terdapat alasan munasabah, namun kelewatan di pihak pendakwaan tidak sepatutnya secara automatik menyebabkan tertuduh terus ditahan.

Beliau turut mencadangkan hakim diberi budi bicara lebih luas untuk membenarkan ikat jamin dalam kes yang ketika ini tidak membenarkannya, termasuk di bawah Seksyen 13 Akta Kesalahan Keselamatan (Langkah-Langkah Khas) 2012 dan Seksyen 41B Akta Dadah Berbahaya 1952.
Peguam S Vinesh bersetuju pihak pendakwaan perlu memastikan siasatan utama, termasuk mendapatkan laporan kimia, diselesaikan sebelum suspek didakwa.

Vinesh berkata Kanun Tatacara Jenayah sudah menetapkan tempoh tertentu bagi pengendalian kes jenayah, termasuk 30 hari untuk persidangan praperbicaraan, 60 hari bagi pengurusan kes dan 90 hari untuk perbicaraan dimulakan selepas tertuduh didakwa.
Katanya, garis panduan lebih jelas dan semakan kehakiman diperlukan bagi menangani kelewatan kerana kesannya bukan sekadar menyebabkan seseorang kehilangan kebebasan.

“Ada keluarga yang mungkin berpecah, perkahwinan gagal dan pendidikan anak-anak terjejas.
"Jika seseorang dibebaskan selepas ditahan selama beberapa tahun, mampukah kita mengembalikan tahun-tahun yang telah hilang itu?” katanya.
52303885b4269406: PETALING JAYA: In a healthy tropical forest, morning is anything but quiet. Birds call, insects hum and, if you are lucky, the long, elaborate songs of gibbons can be heard carrying through the canopy.

But researchers from Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM) studying gibbons have found that groups living near noisy roads appear to call far less often than those in quieter surroundings, raising questions about how traffic and development may alter the soundscape of a forest even when the trees remain standing.

According to a recent report by The Guardian, research led by USM doctoral student Benjamin Galea compared the morning calls of white-handed gibbons at three Malaysian sites with different levels of human disturbance.
The research, which has yet to be peer reviewed, involved recordings taken during the wet and dry seasons in 2023 and 2024.

The results were striking: gibbons living close to a highway called in just 36% of recordings, compared with 71.4% at a quieter seaside location and 84.6% near a hiking trail. Within individual sites, the likelihood of calling also fell as background noise increased.

“Gibbons' songs are not just background noise or a way of announcing their presence,” research supervisor Nadine Ruppert told The Guardian, explaining that their calls can travel for close to 1km through dense vegetation.

"They are important for communication between groups, territorial interactions and social bonds. So when we introduce persistent human-generated noise into their habitat, we are potentially interfering with a very important part of their lives."

This matters because sound is central to how these animals interact over distance. If traffic begins to mask their calls, the experts want to know whether it could affect anything from territory defence and pair coordination to warning others of potential danger.

There may even be consequences beyond the gibbons themselves. Ulrich H Reichard, a professor of anthropology at Southern Illinois University Carbondale who was not involved in the local research, noted that birds and squirrels appear to recognise and respond to gibbon alarm calls.
In that sense, a gibbon's voice is not simply part of the forest soundtrack; it may contribute to a broader network of communication among animals sharing the same habitat.
So, are roads actually silencing them?
Not necessarily, and this is where the findings become more nuanced. One possibility is that heavy traffic simply makes calling less effective because the sound is masked.

Another is that the highway gibbons may be adapting their behaviour by singing earlier, before the monitoring devices began recording at 6am. On some mornings, the researchers found that the animals were already partway through their songs when recording started.

Singing earlier could help them avoid peak traffic noise, although Galea noted that such a change might in turn interfere with resting, feeding or communication with neighbouring groups that are not active at the same time.

The hiking-trail group complicates the picture further. Despite regular human activity, these gibbons called most frequently, possibly because they lived closer to another gibbon group and therefore had greater reason to defend their territory acoustically.
Galea also found evidence that they may adjust how they vocalise when vehicle noise becomes more significant, suggesting that gibbons are not simply passive victims of a changing soundscape.
Even so, plenty remains unknown. As Reichard put it: “One important question that we have to ask is how much calling is necessary for successful communication.”
A forest is more than its trees

What the research does highlight is a form of habitat change that is much harder to see than deforestation. Conservation often focuses on how much forest remains, whether trees are being cleared, and whether animals still have enough physical space in which to survive.
Yet wildlife also experiences its surroundings through sensory cues - which means a forest can remain visibly intact while becoming less suitable in ways humans may barely notice.

A patch of forest may still look green on a map, but if it is hemmed in by roads, housing or industry, its acoustic environment can change substantially. Conservation, therefore, should consider not only how much forest remains, but what animals experience while living within it.

White-handed gibbons are already classified as endangered: their population is believed to have declined by more than 50% over the past 45 years owing to habitat destruction, hunting, capture and other causes.

And while noise pollution is unlikely to be their greatest threat, the USM research suggests it could represent another, less visible pressure on animals already living in increasingly fragmented landscapes.
That makes the study interesting not because it proves traffic is silencing Malaysia's gibbons, but because it raises a broader question about what makes a habitat truly habitable.
0003c31a34b628a7: NEW YORK: Malaysia says it is “sick of” the United Nations Security Council veto repeatedly frustrating efforts to secure action on Gaza, reiterating its call for the veto power held by the council’s five permanent members to be abolished.

Foreign minister Mohamad Hasan said Malaysia and other member states had exhausted every effort in the pursuit of justice for Gaza, including calls for an immediate ceasefire, unrestricted humanitarian aid, punitive action against Israel and full Palestinian membership of the UN.

“Yet, again and again, the collective will of this assembly has encountered the silencing effect of the veto. Malaysia will speak plainly: We are sick of it,” he said when delivering Malaysia’s national statement at the general debate of the 81st UN General Assembly here today.

Mohamad said the need for reform was nowhere more critical than in the Security Council, where the exercise of the veto must be questioned and strongly challenged by every member of the General Assembly, particularly in cases involving crimes against humanity.
He said General Assembly Resolution 76/262, adopted in 2022, had already created an accountability channel between the Security Council and the General Assembly.
“We must make full use of this resolution as a launchpad for greater accountability regarding the use of the veto,” he said.
Mohamad also said that expanding the Security Council’s membership alone would not be enough to address its shortcomings.
“It is the veto that must be challenged, and it is the veto that must be abolished. We must begin the work now,” he said.

Malaysia has previously called for the abolition of the veto while also supporting restrictions on its use in cases involving serious violations of international law if outright abolition cannot be achieved.
At the same time, Malaysia also supported expanding both permanent and non-permanent Security Council membership to make the body more representative.
The Security Council has repeatedly been deadlocked over ceasefire efforts in Gaza, with the US using its veto to block several resolutions despite broad support from other council members.

In June 2025, the US vetoed a draft resolution calling for an immediate and permanent ceasefire in Gaza, despite the other 14 council members voting in favour. The US again vetoed a similar Gaza ceasefire resolution in September that same year.
In closing his speech, Mohamad said the UN must reform institutions that no longer reflected current realities and ensure that the rules of the global system are applied equally to all.
He said Malaysia continued to believe in multilateralism, “most of all, when the alternative is a world ruled by power alone”.
“Malaysia will not turn away from the UN in its hour of difficulty,” he said.
“We will not abandon multilateralism just because it is imperfect. We will do the work to make it worthy of the trust placed in it.”
f68c3be8127ee4f5: PETALING JAYA: The Bar Council’s criminal law committee chairman Vivek Sukumaran has proposed measures to reduce delays in criminal cases, including requiring key investigations to be substantially completed before charges are brought.
Speaking to FMT, Vivek said chemist and forensic reports should generally be ready before a person is charged, as incomplete investigations contribute to delays in bringing cases to trial.

Vivek also proposed prioritising cases involving accused persons in custody, imposing stricter controls on postponements, and conducting regular judicial reviews to determine whether continued detention remains justified.
He said bail should be set according to an accused person’s means, as some people remain in remand for minor offences simply because they cannot raise bail or find a surety.
“No one should be held for more than two years without a verdict unless a judge is satisfied there are compelling reasons,” said Vivek.
He was commenting on an FMT report in which Chief Justice Wan Ahmad Farid Wan Salleh voiced concern over accused persons spending lengthy periods in remand awaiting trial.
Vivek said statutory limits were necessary to prevent accused persons from languishing in custody before trial and to ensure that delays do not undermine the presumption of innocence.

Although a 2017 registrar’s circular sets a 12‑month timeframe for disposing of criminal cases in the sessions and magistrates’ courts, calculated from the date the case is registered, there is no law that compels the authorities to release an accused person whose trial does not begin within expeditiously.
Vivek said this meant an accused could remain in custody for years after being charged while waiting for trial.
He said Malaysia could look to England and Wales, where custody time limits are provided for by legislation, with extensions granted by courts only in exceptional circumstances.
Scotland also has statutory time limits for criminal proceedings involving accused persons in custody, with failure to comply resulting in bail unless the court grants an extension.
Vivek said Malaysia should similarly allow extensions where justified, while ensuring prosecution delays do not automatically result in prolonged detention.

He also proposed giving judges greater discretion to grant bail in cases where it is currently barred, including under Section 13 of the Security Offences (Special Measures) Act 2012 and Section 41B of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952.
Lawyer S Vinesh agreed that prosecutors should ensure that key investigative work, such as obtaining chemist reports, was completed before suspects are charged.
He said prosecutors should take no more than three months to ready their case, failing which they should withdraw the charge.

Vinesh said the Criminal Procedure Code already provides timelines for criminal cases, including 30 days for the pre-trial conference, 60 days for case management and 90 days for the trial to commence after an accused is charged.
He said clearer guidelines and judicial reviews were needed to tackle delays, which can have consequences far beyond the loss of an accused person’s liberty.
“Wrongful detention does not only deprive the accused of his liberty, but can also affect his income and his family life,” he said.
“Some families may be torn apart, with marriages breaking down and children’s education affected. If he is acquitted after several years of being detained, can we give him back the years he lost?”
d9946bd51c25fa67: ORLANDO: Teenage debutants Justin Ellis and Julian Hall both scored as a youthful United States team defeated Peru 4-1 in an international friendly in Orlando on Saturday.
Ellis was one of three teenagers named in United States coach Mauricio Pochettino's starting line-up for his team's first game since the World Cup.

Philadelphia Union's 16-year-old prodigy Cavan Sullivan and New England Revolution's 18-year-old Peyton Miller both started alongside 19-year-old Orlando City striker Ellis in a team showing seven changes to the side beaten 4-1 by Belgium in the World Cup's last 16 in July.
The infusion of youth was quick to make its mark, with Ellis glancing in an inviting free-kick from Gio Reyna after just four minutes in a dream start at his home stadium.
"I've probably been dreaming about this day, like, 500 or 1,000 times in my life since I was five years old," Ellis said afterwards. "I can't even describe. It's just crazy."
Peru got back on level terms after just 15 minutes when veteran striker Gianluca Lapadula cleverly headed home a Yoshimar Yotun cross.
The United States regained the lead in the second half when another teenager -- the 17-year-old substitute Mathis Albert -- burst clear down the left and was knocked to the ground by Jesus Pretell.
Despite the foul beginning just outside the area, Jamaican referee Steffon Dewar pointed to the spot and Malik Tillman stepped up to fire home the penalty for 2-1.

Berhalter then completed the scoring with a thunderous effort from just outside the area in the dying minutes to put the seal on an impressive display for the hosts.
66131f9ac9a2e198: WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump on Saturday rejected a truce deal proposed by Iran that Teheran said could have reopened the Strait of Hormuz to shipping within a week.
The waterway is key to the world's energy supply and is now central to the conflict between the US and Iran, which is at a stalemate after nearly seven months.
"I reject their proposal," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "They made a proposal but I've rejected it."
"They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly. They want to make a deal and I think that's fine. I like making a deal too."

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, who was on his way back to Teheran after attending the UN General Assembly in New York, told CBS News the proposal had been developed "in coordination" with supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, according to an excerpt from the video interview shared by Iranian media.

Iran's plan calls for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon, according to Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who met earlier in the week with Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff.

He said the conditions were the same as those laid out in a memorandum of understanding signed with the US earlier this year, which called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.
On the seventh day of the truce, Iran would reopen Hormuz. Pezeshkian told CBS that the "process will begin from the very day they accept it."

At the UN, Saudi Arabia's Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan complained that the "international community has been absent" and failing to live up to the responsibility to keep the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab open.

"The kingdom rejects any party's use of these vital passages as a tool for pressure, threat, or harm to the interests of states," he said, stressing the waterways' importance to global energy security.

His Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov, told member states that "Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilising this strategically important region."

In New York, Pezeshkian met with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, according to his office, and said: "Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table but, given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States."

Araghchi said at the UN: "Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days."
"The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure," he added.
However, within hours of his comments The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump was skeptical that Teheran would meet his demands and expects to renew the US bombing campaign.
Trump also posted an image to his Truth Social platform of a map showing the Strait of Hormuz circled and labelled "Trump Strait."
Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for Iran's Revolutionary Guards, was quoted by Tasnim news agency as saying: "We will not cease punishing the US until Iran's seven conditions are met."
Mohebi had told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Teheran's demands.
Washington and Teheran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war, to reopen the strait and to launch talks on Iran's nuclear programme.
But the deal broke down shortly afterwards when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.
Iran requires ships to obtain authorisation before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.
Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.

0700a7c47d9d5aa5: NEW YORK was never meant to be on my bucket list.

Perhaps it's because America never felt entirely foreign to me. As a Malaysian, I'd been exposed to so much of it long before I ever set foot there: the movies, music, sitcoms, presidents and instantly recognisable landmarks, along with all those grand ideas about the American Dream and the Land of the Free.
But the America I'd been reading about lately seemed rather different from the one Hollywood sold us.

Donald Trump was back in the White House, immigration enforcement had intensified and tariffs had once again become part of the conversation back home in Malaysia. More recently, controversy erupted after Trump barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, a decision the news organisations challenged on press freedom grounds.
For a Malaysian journalist watching from thousands of kilometres away, America seemed full of contradictions. Yet there was one American icon I'd always wanted to see: the Statue of Liberty.

Blame Hollywood. I've watched enough movies to feel as though Lady Liberty and I go way back. I've seen her half-buried in Planet of the Apes, frozen in The Day After Tomorrow and battered in 2012. Hollywood has drowned her, frozen her and generally subjected the poor woman to more indignities than most movie stars could survive.
And suddenly, unexpectedly, I was going to meet her.
LADY LIBERTY

I was in New York on assignment but, with a little time to myself, decided on a side quest. Armed with ChatGPT and Google Maps, which became my very patient New York guides, I took the train from Newark to the World Trade Centre Transportation Hub, and emerged beneath the magnificent white ribs of the Oculus.

From there, I walked to Battery Park, which turned into rather more walking than I'd anticipated. At some point, I began to wonder whether ChatGPT and Google Maps had conspired to help me achieve my daily step count!

The waterfront walk was beautiful, though, and somewhere along the way I caught my first glimpse of her. There she was in the distance, instantly recognisable, standing in New York Harbour with her torch held high. After years of seeing her in movies, postcards and photographs, the sight of the real thing was unexpectedly breathtaking.
GETTING CLOSER

Naturally, seeing her from afar only made me want to get closer. For US$25.80, about RM109 at the time, my Pedestal Reserve ticket included the ferry, access to the pedestal and Ellis Island. I'd wanted to go all the way up to the crown, but those limited tickets are snapped up quickly and usually need to be booked well in advance.
Soon I was aboard the ferry, trying to look like a seasoned traveller while quietly concentrating on staying upright as the boat bobbed beneath my feet.
It's only a short ride to Liberty Island, but as we drew closer and Lady Liberty grew larger against the skyline, whatever cool journalist persona I might have possessed promptly disappeared.
I gaped, gasped and took far too many photographs, much to the bemusement of fellow passengers who appeared considerably more restrained.
UP CLOSE AND PERSONAL

Officially called Liberty Enlightening the World, the statue was a gift from France to the United States. Designed by French sculptor Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi, with Gustave Eiffel responsible for her internal framework, she was dedicated in 1886.

What intrigued me even more was the story of how her pedestal was funded. America was responsible for paying for it, but the money was running out when Joseph Pulitzer, the Hungarian-born immigrant and publisher of The New York World, launched a fundraising campaign. His newspaper promised to publish the name of every donor, regardless of how little they gave.
The response was extraordinary. In just five months in 1885, about 125,000 people contributed more than US$100,000, much of it in donations of US$1 or less.

There's something wonderfully democratic about an immigrant publisher rallying ordinary people, many of them immigrants themselves, to help complete what would become America's great symbol of liberty.

More than 140 years later, that history carries a certain irony. Immigration is once again at the heart of a fierce American debate, yet some of the hands and small donations that helped Lady Liberty rise above New York Harbour belonged to people who'd arrived in America from somewhere else.
My ticket also took me up to the pedestal observation level, mercifully by lift after all that walking, where the views across New York Harbour towards Manhattan are magnificent.

Back at ground level, the Statue of Liberty Museum tells her story and houses her original torch, removed during restoration in the 1980s. Free ranger-led tours are also available, while an audio tour is included with the ferry ticket.
MOVING FORWARD

Before leaving, I took one last look at Lady Liberty and noticed something I'd somehow missed in all those years of seeing her on screen: broken shackles and chains at her feet, symbolising freedom from slavery and oppression, and her raised right foot, as though she's stepping forward.

Our eyes are naturally drawn upwards towards the crown and that famous torch, but perhaps what lies at her feet matters just as much. For all the contradictions of today's America, she continues to hold aloft an ideal larger than the monument itself.
Lady Liberty matters not because America has always lived up to everything she represents, but because ideals matter precisely when reality falls short of them.
And more than a century after she first raised her torch over New York Harbour, that lifted foot still seems to say something important: there's always further to go.

b0a9bae8afbb255f: PETALING JAYA: Perikatan Nasional may lose its name and logo if it is eventually deregistered, but component members Gerakan and the Malaysian Indian People’s Party (MIPP) are unlikely to stray far from PAS, say political analysts.
Universiti Sains Malaysia’s Sivamurugan Pandian said both parties are likely to remain with PAS if the Islamic party gives them sufficient electoral space and political identity.
Sivamurugan said Gerakan and MIPP would probably prefer PN to survive, but could follow PAS into a new political vehicle if the coalition was deregistered.
“They would like to keep PN, but if Bersatu leans towards PH, the advantage is for Bersatu to keep PN if PN is not deregistered.
“If that is the scenario, PAS, Wawasan, Gerakan and MIPP may activate MN as a new coalition,” he said, referring to Muafakat Nasional.
The Registrar of Societies has suspended PN following a notice issued to the coalition seeking an explanation of a complaint lodged by Bersatu.
RoS said the suspension, which took effect on Sept 23, was intended to safeguard PN's interests and prevent it from continuing to breach its rules.
New coalition if PN goes
Lau Zhe Wei of International Islamic University Malaysia said the relationship among the PN parties mattered more than the coalition’s formal structure.
“Even if PN was dissolved, it would not be a problem. They could simply form another coalition under a different name and recreate the same structure.
“If there is not enough time to establish a new coalition before an election, they could contest under another party’s flag, most likely PAS, or perhaps Wawasan,'' he said.
Lau said the decision by Gerakan and MIPP to stay put in PN suggested that they were more comfortable remaining alongside PAS than aligning themselves with Bersatu.
“If Gerakan or MIPP were genuinely closer to Bersatu and wanted to remain with it, they could leave PN and form another grouping or simply align themselves with Bersatu.
“But that has not happened in recent months. They appear comfortable remaining in PN or, in other words, alongside PAS,” he said.
PAS holds key to smaller parties' future
Sunway University's Wong Chin Huat said the smaller parties were unlikely to dictate what a post-PN arrangement would look like.
“The simple answer is that MIPP and Gerakan don’t matter. They don’t decide. PAS and Wawasan decide.
“If PAS and Wawasan decide to field their candidates in the coming Melaka election, they will get to contest as part of the PAS bloc. Very likely, they would contest under PAS’s flag,” he said.

Wong said any deregistration of PN will essentially have only one effect: the logo used for PN candidates, likely to be replaced by PAS's, which might have lesser appeal to a tiny segment of the electorate.
He said Gerakan and MIPP’s choices would ultimately be guided by electoral necessity.
“Gerakan and MIPP are rational players. They don’t love PAS, Wawasan or Bersatu. They love whichever party can deliver them votes because these parties can’t deliver votes themselves.
“PN’s deregistration doesn’t affect their chances of being fielded. That’s decided by PAS and Wawasan’s strategic calculations,” he said.

8fe2176c252b9762: LONDON: Thomas Tuchel remains convinced England can get over the line against the world's best despite seeing his side blow a second-half lead to lose 3-2 to Spain on Saturday.

2da8e66942f2479e: ON the morning of Sept 15, the ping of my mobile phone startled me awake as I tried to drift back to sleep after Subuh prayers. The message simply read: "Dear Zaharah, it is 6am in London now. But then, you Muslims are early birds! I haven't spoken with you in ages. May I call now? Kandan."
"Caaaan!" I replied, only to regret my informality almost immediately.

When you are communicating with Datuk V.L. Kandan, a product of the Kirkby Malayan Teachers' Training College (MTTC), an educator, a veteran lawyer, and much more, you do not take liberties with your spelling.

There was no time for a mental slap on the wrist. My phone sprang to life again, and I was delighted to hear his voice on the other end of the line; cheerful, though punctuated by bouts of coughing during our seven-minute conversation.
"I am 89, Zaharah, and I have been poorly," he said, explaining the coughs.
After promising to share more stories, we said our goodbyes. It was the last call I would receive from Kandan. It was to be his last call to anyone.

Six days later, I received another WhatsApp message from his number. It was from his daughter, Shakuntala, informing me that her father had died at 2pm on the same day he had called me, barely 40 minutes after our conversation ended.
I was shocked beyond words.

The educator in him remained present until his very last breath. He had wanted to tell me how proud he was of his grandnephew's academic achievements, and he wanted to speak about the importance of education in shaping a person's life.
That final phone call, and the story he was so eager to share, was in itself a testament to what Kandan was all about: an unwavering passion for education.

Even in the final minutes of his life, he was not speaking about his own achievements, whether as a former assemblyman or as a distinguished lawyer with Shearn Delamore & Co, where he earned a reputation as a leading intellectual property practitioner.

No, he wanted to speak about a young person's educational journey, encouraging others, and reminding us of the transformative power of learning. In that sense, Kandan remained an educator to the very end.
I had met Kandan twice, once in 2017 and again in 2019, when he and other Kirkbyites, all in their late 80s, attended their organised reunions at their alma mater in Kirkby.

Kandan was from the fifth batch of teachers despatched to Kirkby to a place he repeated and proudly announced as "the one and only teachers' training college in the world, to be set up in a foreign land, to train teachers for a country that was yet to attain independence. It was not only unprecedented, it was phenomenal!"
The first batch of 149 Malayans arrived on the Blue Funnel in 1952. Three years later, Kandan and the fifth batch arrived on the BOAC Arganout.

When I met the group at the Liverpool train station in August 2017, it was like meeting a group of schoolchildren on their first outing; excitement and nostalgia etched on their faces. Kandan and several others wore blazers proudly displaying the Kirkby training college emblem, exchanging shared experiences of yesteryear.

It was a historic gathering in Granborne Chase, the site of their alma mater, to unveil a plaque honouring the spot where, on Feb 7, 1956, Tunku Abdul Rahman Putra Al-Haj announced the date of the country's independence to about 300 students of the MTTC — a site in North West England that is now a piece of Malaysia's history.
Kandan and his fellow Kirkbyites were among the first to hear the historic announcement after Tunku and his delegation returned from the successful negotiations at Lancaster House.
This was a story, among others, that Kandan proudly and repeatedly narrated to his family.
"The plaque was not simply about remembering where Kirkby once stood, but about remembering what Kirkby stood for and carrying that spirit forward," said Renuka, Kandan's second daughter.

It was Renuka who took Kandan to Kirkby as his 78th birthday treat in 2015. It was during this visit that he went to a grocery store he frequented in the 1950s and found a card appealing for information on the Kirkby Teachers' Training college. Kandan then made his way to the Knowsley Resource Centre —and the rest is history.

"I think my father's lifelong commitment to education can be traced back to his beginnings as a teacher. Although he eventually left the classroom to pursue a career in law, I don't think he ever stopped thinking of himself as an educator.

"Kirkby and his early teaching years instilled in him a belief that education was one of the most powerful ways of changing a young person's life and, through them, the future of the country," said Renuka, who now lives in Brighton.

Among the tributes for the late Kandan was a story from someone whose life was significantly impacted by his passion for education. Sumiita Devi Panirselvan, a former student of SJKT Ladang Raja Musa, Kuala Selangor, had scored 7A's in her UPSR examination, making her the first student in her school to achieve that milestone.
In a touching tribute, she wrote about Kandan's visit to the estate.
"He made a solemn promise to support any student from SJKT Ladang Raja Musa who achieved outstanding results, and he kept that promise.
"For a child growing up in Raja Musa Estate, meeting a leader of his stature was a profound and unforgettable moment.

"His visit did more than simply celebrate my academic achievement; it gave me a new sense of confidence and instilled in me a lasting determination to excel in my higher education", wrote Sumiita, an engineering geologist.
Kandan's impact, she said, extended far beyond her own life.

"His presence and financial support inspired the entire community, proving to the children of the estate that their dreams were within reach. He passionately believed that the younger generation could uplift themselves and transform their lives through education."
I wish Kandan had shared this story with me, but the man hailed as a gentle giant wasn't one to speak about his achievements.
"Serendipity" was one of his favourite words, Renuka recalled.

Indeed, his discovery of that small postcard in a village grocery store window, which eventually brought him and his fellow Kirkbyites back to the place he called his Camelot, seemed an act of serendipity.

So too, perhaps, was the final phone call he made to me that morning, a last conversation that perfectly reflected the values by which he lived: education, encouragement and hope for the next generation.
